the female elephants of the herd consider hope to be poison during the separation from the leader of the herd, whose face is dejected and who has been struck down by the lord of serpents, enraged by the lifting of the mountain, as he rests upon his expanded hoods.

The more the earth is shaken, the more it becomes capable of supporting the weight of the monkeys' bodies; though shaken, it remains unshakable, with its mountain peaks shattered by the impact of their arms and their rocky masses dislodged from both the summits and the slopes.
The sky appears as if raised up, the horizons as if drawn far away,
and the surface of the earth as if pulled out by the monkeys who are uprooting the mountains; it is filled with deep chasms where the mountain ranges, destroyed by the hosts of monkeys, have fallen.

The mountain-ambrosia tree, scattered with the radiance of the jewels on the hoods of the remaining serpents, has lightened even the heavy arm-strength of the Lord of the Nishacharas— which had been witnessed as superior on Kailasa—
by means of the monkeys who, one by one, lifted up mountains.
The netherworld has become one where the masses of darkness mingle with the radiance of the sun as it descends into the mountain clefts;
it has become thinned of gloom and grey with rising smoke, while the monkeys,
acting without hesitation, have completed the uprooting of the mountain dwellings.
With their sole essence devoted to the master’s business,

even those who are great become light when they are vessels of glory; the masses of mountains, whose broad bases rest upon the tips of the monkey-chiefs’ arms, have their waterfalls cast far away by the winds rushing forth in haste.
Then, having seized the entire multitude of mountains with their arms, the monkeys leapt into the sky with ease even from the foothills;
though they were agile,
free from fear, light in their flight, and yet heavy due to their vast size, they departed without making a sound.
In a single leap, the monkeys leaped over the sky as if it were great mountains;

they traversed the earth's circumference, which was joined together by the mouths of rivers that had been blocked by mountains, and which was being formed as the waters rushed forth from their uneven heights, broke apart, flowed on, and then turned back.
The forests are bewildered by the elephants, whose great tusks are like mountains, who have turned back after fleeing in terror;
they are gazed upon with startled, wide-eyed looks as the elephants momentarily turn their heads,
while the trees— already uprooted, fallen, or being lifted— are cast straight away.
The river currents, having set out along the paths of the mountains whose kings have departed,
agitate the sky where the essence of the clouds has been crushed;
the mountain ranges are split apart by the openings [of the rivers], and the sun is obscured as it revolves around the peaks.
With mountains placed upon their shoulders, with peaks grasped by upraised right hands,
and with the expanse of their hips supported by the palms of their outstretched left hands, the monkeys turn back even from the very start—
that which was not within the power of those who had previously rushed forth by the strength of their arms alone.
That very same sky now serves as the refuge for those poets and great mountains alike;
for the host of monkeys traverses the mountain peaks,
whose bases are joined together when lifted up simultaneously, and whose river-mouths are scraped away by the friction of their summits as they rise one after another.
Having gazed for a long time, the clouds drift on, weary from the burden of the mountains;
they resemble the ocean, occupying the sites of the great mountains that were first uprooted,
with their cloud-banks momentarily joined together and established by the mountain-rivers tossed up by the wind.
Increasing in volume, they flow like the currents of great rivers across the vault of the sky;
upon the peaks, the lofty crags are like conch-shells joined with their tusks;
scattered among the agitated mountain torrents, the forest herds do not emerge even when the waters have subsided.

The mouths of the mountain caves, whose chests were heaving with agitation and whose slender waists were visible through the mountain clefts, closed as if in a fragrant inhalation of the pollen of flowers; meanwhile, the winds held the trembling serpents in their palms, breaking them apart against the face of the sky.
On the peaks split open by the weight of the earth, they stabilize the mountains with their second hands; the mountain torrents,
which had been diverted from their courses by the mountain peaks being carried away by monkeys fleeing the impact against the surface of the sky, become for a moment side-streams of great rivers.
In the mountain ranges, where masses of rain-clouds emerge from the slopes of the peaks amidst thickets of banyan trees,
and where herds of elephants sit within the caves of the aged sandalwood forests,
the mountain flows with its peaks obscured by crags being carried away by monkeys rushing in their haste.
Following the path of their shadows with speed, like monkeys leaping from the slopes of Mount Malaya,

those poets who had observed the great mountains, scrutinized them, and even uprooted them, did not place them in the ocean; for they were neither seen, nor grasped, nor brought down by those who had approached them.
Filled with the wreckage of shattered trees, made uneven by uprooted and fallen crags,
and reaching the ocean, the torrent of the monkeys appears like a second crossing of the Ganges,
having seized mountains and being repeatedly cast back as it overflows its banks.
The monkey host, its eyes blossoming with passion as it turned toward Rāma, has been described.
Thus ends the sixth [and seventh] canto in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha* composed by the illustrious Pravarasena.

Then those monkeys began to construct a bridge, marked by the eternal fame of Rāma, its peak capable of surpassing the sin of the Ten-faced one through the power of their valor; however, the great mountains held upon the surface of the earth were released back into the ocean.
When the mountain masses fell from afar, the earth’s surface—torn up by the submersion of the forests as if by the arms of the Primal Boar—was not seen; when they shook, it trembled;
when they fell for a moment, it was agitated; and when they sank, the ocean swelled.

The water of the great ocean, having its aquatic creatures overturned and its shores dragged across as it roamed through the forests, became dark with the hue of jars; as it surged forth for the first time,
the mountains were submerged by the waters, yet once again the masses of mountains reappeared, their forms unseen until they met [the shore].
The expanse of the sky-ocean appears as if it were a mountain thus fashioned;
mountains have been weighed, the ocean has been churned by monkeys, and fear has been produced in their enemies—
for indeed, even the mere undertakings of those with great fortune are heavy, not merely their hearts' core.
That which appears as a mountain is known by this [water] to be bound; furthermore, where have those growing in the ocean gone? They are known by the water to be the earth itself.
Vast with its encirclement of the entire world, its path for the sun’s chariot obstructed by thousands of peaks—
Even that lofty mountain has perished like a blade of grass within the mouth of the *timiṅgila* fish; whatever water rises from the mountain peaks toward the vault of heaven appears,
together with its jewels, like a falling circle of stars.
Driven by monkeys, surrounded by their own broad, swirling spray,
these mountain peaks wander even before reaching the ocean as if in circles of eddies;
their monkey populations, momentarily scattered and cast away, vanish into the intervals between the summits.
The mountain ranges first fall into the sky and later into the ocean; long, wide, and winding, they roar as they are filled with wind in the sea,
their mountain torrents plunging with speed into the depths of the underworld.

Thousands of mountains, their peaks shattered by the fragments of split rocks and greyed by the pollen of flowers shaken from their own trees, fall into the ocean of jewels like terrified Vajrapāṇis, each one released and striking the sky as they descend.
First the mountains fall, and afterwards the great river currents; their uneven courses of movement visible as they are divided within the pure waters,
the great mountains vanish only after a long time, observed by the monkeys stationed motionless upon them.
With rays of light trembling like filaments emerging from flowers of foam,
they suggest the ocean as it flows with its roots agitated; the jewels shake the earth as if it were the shore, and they shatter the mass of mountains as if it were the world's end.
The mountain ranges—
whose tree-sprouts are bent back by the swaying intervals of their branches, whose waters are uprooted,
and whose waterfalls are turned downward— are overturning the earth; they seize the sky as if it were fear, and release the netherworld as if it were their natural state.
The mountain peaks, which had been darkened by the dense masses of water falling from the great mountains as they crumbled,
now reveal themselves as they fall; their echoes are stirred by the ocean,
and their tufts of manes are slightly washed, while their faces are smeared with the mountain minerals heated by the waters.
The monkeys retreat, their shoulders heaving as they lift up the great mountains;
lightened by the bursting forth of waterfalls and with the trees on their peaks tossed upward by the wind,
those mountains, hurled aloft by the leaping monkeys, fall from their summits into the ocean.
The mountain paths, where masses of water are turned back as they break through, are covered with flowers;

they are tawny with turmeric and possess the sweet-smelling fragments of trees falling from the elephants' temples; and they appear wrathful, as the mountain peaks are struck by the elephants who are startled by the water.
The forest buffaloes, with their eyes like ripe mangoes rolling and turning in single circles as they shake themselves,
break apart even when joined together; yet, comforted by looking at one another,
the herd of deer, their bodies drawn along by the waves of the mountain-streams rising and falling, breaks apart once more.
With their temples split by tusks, the elephant-lions, dragged by the steady trunks of the lions,
roar as their mouth-caverns gape with blood containing pearls; the lion-elephants,
having overturned the elephants, fall down, their fury intensified by the collapse of the mountain.
With their bodies weakened by sleeplessness caused by the exhaustion of the hunt,

even the female elephants wandered through the trees like forest creepers; they wound themselves with paths that swirled around the mouths of mountain caves, which were filled with scattered sprouts and young shoots.
As the mountain ranges are being uprooted and cast down simultaneously upon the earth and the ocean, the netherworld (*pātāla*) is incessantly opened;
they are tossed about and turned, encircled by rows of gurgling, cascading waterfalls.
The hosts of monkeys, their thick masses entwined and the mountain vines clinging to them, fall as the great mountains crash against one another;
with the edges of the rocks shattered by the flailing of their own arms,
they move on with their manes disheveled, rising up into the sky with water sprayed from their leaps.
Again and again, the surface of the sky appears like the underworld filled with streams of water cast down by the mountain's impact;
and the vast expanse of the underworld appears like the opening of the sky,
its bosom strewn with lotus forests uprooted from the earth’s surface, which has been shattered by the upheaval and drenched by the falling waters.
The great mountains fall with their peaks shattered and crumbling as they are seized by the helpless elephant of the ocean;
the mountain-shore, split by the impact of the peaks, groans; the ocean, stumbling on its uneven edge, retreats and reaches a state of exhaustion, yet it does not vomit forth the nectar-essence.
With its mountains uprooted and leveled, where the terrible cries of those cast into the turbulent ocean resound,
how can there be a means of reaching the city of the Rākṣasas, which involves such a dreadful undertaking—
a whirlwind that has torn up the sky, causing golden rocks to flash and spin through the air?
The mountain range, its valleys fragrant with flowers, is overturned by the force of the wind;
the clamor of the mountains increases; the ocean, its face turned by the swirling tempest, surges;
and the mountain peaks, their trees stripped bare by the gale, fall down with their waterfalls standing upright.
Driven from afar, their bodies crushed and mangled as they are swept along by the current,
the great river-fish, tossed violently into the ocean, gasp out a bitter sound;
with their venomous-jewel-like eyes bulging, they sprawl upon the shifting, uneven surface of the waves.
With the sunbeams obscured by the masses of trees above and the mountain caves covered by the rays of the sun,

the lord of serpents, having turned back toward the ocean whose waters were dried up by the mountain torrents, somehow managed to encircle the earth— which was as unstable as the tip of a balance-beam— by coiling his body.

The earth, the bearer of mountains, has forgotten at once the fear of faults caused by the trampling of the hooves of the primordial boar; and the ocean has remembered its agitation during the churning,
as if remembering its own pain from being churned while dwelling in the Malaya sandalwood groves.

Struck by the peaks of the mountains, the lord of rivers flows down through the fault of the Ten-faced one; as the mountains, submerged in the mass of water, rise up again, he— reddened like crushed coral—
is scattered over the ridges like a cloud of dust from pulverized minerals, with its spray rising in a dense mass.
The ocean water resounds as it flows over the mountains, its waves agitated by the peaks of the crags;
it flows with the surging currents colored by the liquid essence of minerals that have dissolved, and it overflows with the juices of sandalwood trees and medicinal herbs shattered by the force.
As the mountain peaks collapse, their broad branches and leafy thickets fall, their roots submerged in the upsurging waters.
Leaping with lightness, the trees, though unsupported, cling to the sky;
by the power of the monkeys, who are filled with royal pride and terrified by the clouds split asunder in the sky,
the waters of the ocean are shattered by the mountains whose lower lips are clearly pushed back by their bared white teeth.
With its cave mouths filled by the wind, its rocky enclosures shattered by the force of the wind,
the mountain peak falls into the expanse of the sky, pregnant with Indra’s bow [the rainbow] rising from the mountain cascades;
it is overwhelmed by the roar of the water-filled torrents as they collide against other rocks.

Do not the mountain peaks, with their many trees and groves, fall down in great numbers? They appear as if they were the very leaves themselves, torn away by the violent impact against the ocean, their blood-like foam spreading out and mingling with the tips of yak-tail fans.
Out of fear of the Siddhas, the groves of trees release their blossoms;

the mountain rivers lose their mouths as their waters dry up; the ocean’s waters whirl about; and the quarters of the sky spin, with the Lord of Elephants raising his trunk to ward off the approaching eclipse.
Rāvaṇa casts his gaze upon the herds of elephants approaching with their mouths like gaping whirlpools, having emerged from the Vaitaraṇī river;

as he looks at those rivers whose banks are entwined by the massive peaks of mountains falling headlong toward them, and whose waters are tossed by the force of winds swirling through the gaps between them,
his heart alone suffers, for he knows that they are the very same rivers that separated him from Sītā.
The masses of water, their coral forests scorched by the flames and their conch shells blackened by fire, rise up;
their cities are submerged as they are dragged down to the underworld,
while the mountains— whose flanks are split by the weight of their own overturning— have their aquatic creatures cowering in fear.

The netherworld (pātāla) is seen with its waters divided and its serpents awakened; the elephants, having turned back from the mouths of the agitated ocean, stumble as they descend from the great mountains situated on their flanks;
fixed upon the great elephants, they fall, while the great elephants receive them.

Nor do the great mountains, though tossed by the tempest and heavy with their broad slopes, sink to the bottom of the underworld as they are carried away by the mass of water surging upward; rather, they pass on with their multitudes of trees uprooted and their great fish fainting from the mountain crashes.

The waves of the ocean water, dashed against the coastal rocks, break upward; and from the mountain’s caverns— its peaks shattered as the herds of elephants, distressed by the half-submerged [rocks], flee upward— it is known at once that the divine couple has emerged like the very life-breath of the sky.
The mountains are held up by the arms, the trees by the mountains, and the masses of clouds by the trees;
it is not even known whether the monkeys are binding a bridge or measuring the expanse of the sky.

Released one after another with great haste, they turn, shake off, and fall with their jeweled rocks; the mountain peaks crash into the ocean, crushing the netherworld (rasātala) as its hoods are broken by the trampled great serpents whose shells have been forced open. The mountain peaks devastate the netherworld.

That water of the ocean which perishes— terrible with the falling of mountains from the massed piles of crushed emeralds— is indeed the dreadful fruit for him who gazes on, overwhelmed by the tears of his wife as she is carried off by the King of the Nishādas;
yet, in its place, the broad expanses of the leaders of the jewel-mines are pulverized upon the mountain peaks,
filling the vault of heaven with clouds of unceasing rain, like rows of swans amidst the girdles of forest ranges.

The netherworld licks [the earth], the ground cracks open, and masses of water well up; the courtyard of the sky is filled with smoke, and the mountains are uprooted. Struck down by the mountains, the ocean also rolls for a long time upon the dry land.

With its branches still clinging to the trees, the row of trees fallen into the sea—with their fresh sprouts like an ornament of flowers—becomes adorned with thick, white pearls emerging from the midst of split shells. Thus, the rows of trees become garlands of coral.
The forests, crushed by the gods who dwell upon the great mountains,

proclaim themselves with clouds made of flower-pollen; the hosts of monkeys carry the woods, which are overflowing with the fragrance of honey dripping incessantly, the sky fills with blossoming [trees], and the ocean receives them.
Although the mountains are indeed great, the monkeys nevertheless agitate the netherworld, which has its vast interior far away;

they stir the ocean, which satisfies the buffalo with mud from the mountains slightly shattered, where the forests of coral trees are joined by the trees [on the shore], and where the terrestrial crocodiles mingle with the aquatic creatures.
The forest, where lions are awakened by the scent of the rutting elephants and roar in opposition;
where the herds of elephants turn back in fear as the mountain peaks fall before them;
and which is strewn with yellow leaves, withered and fallen from the forest floor through the process of decay.
The fish swirl about, exhausted by the bitter taste of the sap flowing from the broken trees of passion;

the clusters of creepers are tenderly tossed as their sprouts and leaves are bent by the weight of the mountain; and the poison-colored flowers wither, struck by the wind of the spreading poison-colored breath.
The sky is filled with the spray from mountain peaks whirling in eddies;
the poison of the serpents, overwhelmed by the scent of medicinal herbs falling [from the mountains], surges up in distress;
and the mountain ridges are rendered invisible as they are bent over by the circular whirlpools.

The bridge-causeway, constructed by joining together mountains that were brought down in an unbroken, continuous, and uninterrupted stream, appears to be fashioned from the sky; it is being swallowed by the light of the jewels on the expanded hoods of the serpents of the netherworld as they move about, and it vanishes as it falls into the ocean.

The monkeys, exerting themselves with increasing effort to seize it, [failed] as if through passion turning to aversion; thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Bridge-Building Capable of Joining Lanka."
The eighth consolation:
the yoke-pair.
Thus, when the masses of smoke from the celestial chariots—cleansed by the mountain peaks and waterfalls—are falling down, [the clouds] appear like yoke-pairs.
Then the poets established those great mountains at the edge of the shore— mountains whose extent was like the sky and the ocean,
which had been reduced to mere remnants,
their peaks shattered and overturned by the claws of the trembling [elephants], and whose majesty was perceived only for a moment.
Released from the agitation of the mountains, exhausted, and having failed to reach their first destination,

the surging masses of ocean water— gentle with slow swaying, as if merely going and returning— break apart as they form whirlpools, while the great mountains that had been circling within one eddy scatter as they wander into another.
Though agitated by the terror of seizing the earth, the ocean withdraws its waters; its roar ceases,
and it appears for a moment difficult to discern as it slowly retreats toward its proper place, its surface becoming calm once more.
The water is seen subsiding, with pearls for its budding flowers, filled with circular ripples like emerald bangles, its young shoots mingled with coral, and its white lotuses accompanied by conchs;
it appears as the flowers, tossed about, momentarily emerge from the depths and float back to the surface.
In the whirlpool of the ocean where the redness of dawn is fading,
the elephants and deer— overwhelmed by the scent of the forest-dwelling beasts and distressed by the oncoming wind— return once more,
their faces being fanned by the lions held in their own trunks.
The mouths of the rivers have become turbid from the breaking of trees, their pale foam shattered by the bitter taste [of the wood]; grey with the dust raised by the surging and swirling currents,
they are like fragments of the Malaya cliffs cast out by the agitated ocean onto the slopes of Mount Mahendra.
In the Malaya ridges, the slopes of Mount Mahendra appear like masses of crushed elephant herds;
they are vast and white, with rounded surfaces where the waves have subsided and receded, resembling the thick down of autumn clouds, with pearl-like sandbanks clinging closely and continuously.
Having caused the ocean to become silent with its roar stilled,
and having cast back the masses of water that had been tossed up by the mountain and long observed, he—
his eyes bestowed upon Nala as he sat upon a seat of shifting jeweled slabs— speaks.
The lord of monkeys, his left arm raised and bearing the weight of the bow,
exhausted the host of monkeys; yet the earth-girdle, with its distant and sparse mountains,
does not appear to have a bridge across it— lest the heavy bow of Rāma be bent once again.
Is wine the moon? Is it nectar? Is it Lakṣmī with her Kaustubha gem?
Or is it the wish-fulfilling tree? Yet, having uttered these things, they were not bestowed by the Ocean of Jewels;
even today, their mere names continue to smoke as they remain far from his body.

O steadfast one, bind that bridge with Rāma’s arrows— which extinguish the fire by the sound of the water-snakes hissing as they enter— so that today itself the Malaya and Suvela mountains may become two distinct banks at the far ends of the ocean.
Then Nala, his splendor clearly emerging from the mass of his supernatural knowledge through the power of his flight, spoke before the lord of monkeys;
his eyes wide with fear and agitation at the sudden alarm of the monkey-king, he said:
"O Lord of Monkeys, speak confidently before the Lord of the Raghus."
The confidence you have inspired in me by the bond of our friendship shall not prove false:
the mountain range has been leveled, the underworld crushed, and the ocean dried up;
today, as it were, my very life has been surrendered, and your confidence has been fulfilled.

Behold that bridge, a marvel upon the earth, constructed like a great island within the circle of the world-ocean; with the Suvela and Malaya mountains joined together as its piers, will it not cross the sea by means of a continuous causeway formed by mountains being joined one after another?

He said: "O monkeys, behold that army! Having crossed the circle of the earth with its dust raised, let it shake the ocean like a mouthful of food, as if Mount Malaya itself were setting out for Suvela and returning again, obstructed by the strength of my arms."

I shall construct a bridge across the surface of the sky, capable of supporting the passage of monkeys rushing with speed, composed of mountain peaks arranged in successive rows and joined together; and upon it, let the ocean waters be rendered motionless, established as if fixed above its inner depths.
O water-bearing clouds, form a bridge across the ocean; O mountains of the netherworld,
follow my path and construct the causeway according to your respective duties, casting aside the great rocks,
so that this bridge— free from the defects seen in previous attempts— may quickly become a bond of happiness.
That monkey army— delighted by Nala’s words, having cast off their clamor due to the exhaustion and fatigue that had subsided,
and moving with such force that they seemed to lift the earth and fill the ten directions— was ready for action.
Then, having bathed slowly in the water of his father with a pleasant touch,
and having first paid homage to the feet of Rāma and afterwards to the Sun, he—
his mouth-like cave filled with the branches of an *aśoka* tree bearing sprouts that resembled molten gold— [emerged].
Just as the first auspicious water-pot was set down by Nala in the ocean,
so too was that mountain first released by Nala, situated upon the shore,
appearing like the very beginning of the bridge intended for the ruin of Laṅkā.
And thus the ocean, its waters scattered by the blows of the mountains, churned in the sky;

it washed the faces of the quarters, which were soiled with the dust of the mountain peaks, while the paths of its formation became imperceptible as the quarters were drenched with water and began to coalesce.
Even the great mountains, though their forms are as turbulent as the agitated ocean, do not abandon one another;

for those very paths by which the rivers enter the coastal forests, having encountered the mountains fallen there, become the very same paths by which they emerge, even when their waters are directed toward the opposite shore.
The lofty peaks, released by the monkeys, fall headlong into the fire; though heavy at their base, they whirl about in the conflagration just as they were uprooted.
Shaking them, the mountain-tops strike the faces of the lordly elephants, whose trunks are firmly planted like spikes.

The lions, their manes disheveled by the intense pain of being struck by the frontal globes of elephants, know only the forest elephants with their faces smeared by salt water, whose trunks have been severed and crushed by the elephants’ trunks extended out at the scent of the lions.

Having flown up, the monkeys, their bridge-construction efforts now frustrated, seize the mountain-peaks that had been launched from the ocean; they hold them with their chest-cavities joined by their interlocked palms,
while Nala also binds them, his mane bristling and quivering at that instant.

The mountain that supports the earth— lifted by the hand of Hari when he extended his arm as if it were a mere straw, and which closed the opening in the ground after the ocean had been cast out by many mountains— is alone able to withstand that torrential downpour, standing firm and expanded even further.
The hosts of monkeys place each mountain peak they have obtained from the ocean before them;
having stepped forward, they fix it right there, and thus the bridge is constructed simultaneously by those released from the mountains as it falls evenly upon the path of the bridge.
Nala, having received the mountains, piles them up and arranges them level; the ocean,
its waters surging, increases before him as he constructs the mountain-bridges with the mountain-sections joined by the power of his majesty.
Whatever mountain Hanumān brings, its peaks polished by the sun,
moon, and stars, Nala effortlessly places upon the ocean with his left hand,
creating a bridge of mountains whose summits are strewn with broad lotuses and where the construction of the causeway proceeds with ease.
The earth, supported by the netherworld and clinging to the ocean’s foam, is held fast; bound along the shore of the tide and shaken by the spray of retreating waters,
the forest grove— its branches trembling with shimmering rays— is swaying like the luster of emeralds.
The black serpents clinging to the tusks of the elephants and horses, tossed about by the collisions of the beasts agitated by panic,
fall like fragments of dark mountain peaks; and that very serpent which was first driven back into the ocean by the falling of the mountains now returns.
Likewise, at the edge of the water, the crocodiles— whose flow of rut-fluid falls unbroken as they are startled by the ocean agitated by Nala’s passage— turn their faces away and block the path;
with serpents clinging to their tails, they are like ropes being dragged along by the king.
The waves, possessing pure radiance like sapphires, with masses of emeralds slightly split open and filled with the juice of fruit, and white with foam as pale as a crushed bed of conch shells,
are being tossed about; and as much as the ocean is diminished by the mountains that are simultaneously colliding with it, so much is it restored.

The disturbances of the earth cause the sky to tremble as if it were being shaken; they surge upward just so much as to fill the roots of the mountains with uprooted water, causing the mountain peaks to slip from their foundations, the river mouths to burst open, and the oceans to sway.

When the ocean is driven far away, the bridge-causeway is perceived as being "constructed": it provides a momentary pleasure to the heart of Hari, who has half-way given up his effort; it causes the mountains to fall halfway down; and it makes the waters of the sea sink halfway down into the subterranean realm.
Even as it recedes, this ocean appears to have only just begun to rise,

for it still seems to fill the underworld; nor do the footprints left by the Great Boar, which offered relief to the ocean and were marred by the trampling of the enraged elephants of the quarters, fill [the space].

As the ocean carries away the mass of mountains situated far apart, it stirs up the sea water— which is reddened by the fresh sprouts from the crumbling slopes of the mountains and fragrant with the resin from broken trees— making it appear as if the very essence of the ocean were being churned forth.
In such a way that the crest of its splendor shines, the dam-foundation—filling the hollows and remaining firm—is being constructed;
does it fall as if fashioned from the vault of heaven? Is it being drawn out from the Malaya mountains, long since prepared?
Does it take shape within the waters of the ocean? Having been formed, does it emerge from the subterranean realms? Thus proceeds the construction of Nala’s bridge.
The ocean water in the sky, the surface of the sky in the netherworld when freed from water,
and the mass of mountains seen simultaneously in all three— the sky, the water,
and the netherworld— the ocean, bound by the chains of the coastal forests, has tasted even that which resides in the netherworld.

Just as a wild elephant in rut shakes its tethering post while circling it, so too do the great mountains, drenched by the waters agitated by the monkeys' leaps, being pushed back with great force, each one moving further away from the next.
The mountain peaks fall, their branches stripped by the wind and their jewels scattered; the hosts of men are crushed by fear.
The ocean is agitated and roars, as if unable to contain its swelling tide of intense terror.
Driven far away, it seems to fill the rivers with its surge, or rather, it is churned up, muddied by the falling mountains.
The ocean seems to stop as if turned back by the brilliance of the jewels;

the masses of forest-dwelling elephants, provoked by the scent of ichor and enraged, rush together toward one another upon the causeway, like mountains fallen into the sea when it was churned by the tusks of elephants and the trunks of lions.
Having uprooted masses of trees and long since crushed the slopes of the sandalwood forests,
the waves— streaked with the stains of mineral dust— travel far and then surge upward;
the ocean appears together with many herds of elephants whose eyes are wide with fear at the falling of the mountains.
Just as the water that has overflowed the banks of rivers surges back when the roar of the mountain torrent fills the flood,
so too does this family surge up, having undertaken a great endeavor fashioned by a multitude of mountains that have parched the entire surface of the earth.
The eastern shore of the ocean was darkened by the impact of its own shadow;
the hindquarters of fish were cast up by the forceful blows from the uneven surfaces of the rocks;
and the enclosures of the rocks were torn apart by the crushing pressure of serpents whose bodies had been severed in the middle.
The water of the mountain torrents, which follows the path of elephants startled by the agitation of lions uprooting boulders;
the water of the clouds, resonant as they move along the mountain peaks where they have settled;
and the water of the great cascades, split into two streams as they fall into the hollows and are blocked by wild elephants.
They construct the path for Nala, which—by the fragments of the Malaya peaks known from the sandalwood forests situated between the earth and the sky;

by the rows of trees hanging down as they are uprooted and overturned by the force of the winds opposing the current; and by the ocean being tossed about as it enters through the gaps between the rugged summits—forms a continuous track.
The bridge-extension spreads out; the ocean, struck by the mountain, surges;
the monkey army, having seen the slope of Mount Suvela, roars with its echoes filling the quarters;
and the leaders of the bridge-extension are seen in the midst of the sea where the waters have been parted.
Dragged away in confusion, their mountain wings crushed by fear and scattered,
the monkeys once again bind the path of Nala, which has retreated slightly and whose base is disfigured by the water agitated by the blows from the mountains.
Just as the excellent bridge-arch, having conquered the ocean, becomes closer to it,
so too does the water struck by the mountain rise high above the bridge; though it falls from afar,
it is scattered by its thinness as it stumbles upon the arch.
Those very masses of water become the currents of great rivers, winding and uneven; and the bridge-path,
casting its shadow over the entire expanse of the ocean filled with schools of whales fleeing in terror to the second shore,
bestows its shade upon the slopes of the Suvela mountain as it slightly closes in.
When Nala shook the great mountain, which was firmly rooted and situated on uneven ground, then the ocean—
its entire wealth of gems exhausted— returned after a long time,
reeling from the blows of the rocks hurled by the hosts of monkeys who were delighted by their swift dispatch.
Like the ocean at the mouth of a river, held for a moment between the causeway and Mount Suvela, as the peak of the bridge-path was constructed by the bull-like monkeys,
so too was the heart of the Ten-faced one rent asunder along with the waters of the sea.
With its base meeting the underworld and its river-like current flowing without interruption,

Mount Suvela— though standing firm— fell into the mouth of the mountain-rampart as it was being moved by the lord of the monkeys, who, though situated on the flank of Malaya, stood close to the side of Rāghava.
By his cry, the bridge was known to be filled by the westernmost mountain;
when it began, the entire ocean became uneven in three parts; when it was half-finished, it became twofold; and once completed, that very same ocean became manifold again and again.
The great bridge-arch, its weight increased by the burden of swaying monkeys,
appears as if held up by one tree against another; it stretches across Mount Trikuṭa, making the eastern and western quarters of the great bridge-path seem joined together at their ends.

The causeway, appearing like the path of the sun’s chariot— its sides turned toward Oṛvvatoha, its uneven middle cast upward, and bending as if toward the sky— is established in the ocean waters that resemble the firmament, reaching from Mount Malaya to Mount Suvela, visible as it rises and sets.

The causeway is seen like a great mountain rising up with its broad, outstretched slopes, its massive peaks standing firm amidst the ocean tossed by the wind; it brings about dejection, heavy sighs, loss of sleep, paleness, and weakness.
While the bridge was being built, those [shadows] which had been reflected from Rāma onto Rāvaṇa were now led to their destruction along with the Ten-faced one;
then the bridge-causeway, broad, lofty,
and vast, spread out like the arm of the beloved, having made the ocean its moat.
By the uneven [arrow] made uneven by its flight, heavy as a mountain, and heavy with the audacity of battle—
even from afar— the heart of Daśānana is seen pierced as if by a stake; bees cling to it like a mass of flowers floating in the waters of the agitated ocean.
In some places, trees with young shoots curling upward against the slopes of the mountains appear like the banks of a lake where the ocean has stilled;
elsewhere, crystal rock-slabs fallen between the mountains look like a bridge-construction hope severed in the middle.
Even when covered by falling snow, the peaks of Malaya,
the lord of mountains, are clearly recognized in the conflagration by their fragrance, like crushed sandalwood;
their broad expanse has become manifest, shimmering as they are drenched by the retreating waters of the clouds.

Even in the ocean, the paths of the shoreline where the hosts of lions seize their prey together appear as they emerge from the water; having fallen upon the rocks to tear them apart, they stand on the slopes of the causeway, exhausted by the weight of their mane drenched with water, barely visible.
Having seen their former abodes on the eastern and western slopes, the elephants— whose expansion was previously restricted by the sea— are no longer seen returning to their mountain homes;
they appear like clouds of mineral dust, with white torrents of water scattered by the wind trailing behind them.
The monkey army set forth, its peaks towering like the summits of mountains rising from the surface of the sea,
with the ocean-path constructed and the great mountains placed upon the land exceeding the path of the sea;
it moved with the joy of battle being instilled by Rāghava’s heart as he himself moved.
They fall, stumbling, into the ocean— the abode of Makaras— which has its expanse diminished by the water drawn out for crossing,
and whose supply of water is cut off as it is poured out through the mouths of the crocodiles.
O young man!
Upon the fire of Nala, which possesses lotuses white as conch-shells and displays the appearance of green sprouts of emerald,
with young shoots mingled with coral and a bridge established across its rising banks,
the monkey host traverses; the line of the causeway bows down like a mountain spreading out.
The ocean, whose waters reach the netherworld and which is heavy with all its strength, supports [the bridge];
it moves its hips and bears upon itself a mass of wave-hands;
like a forest elephant tied to a pillar, the ocean is bound to the causeway-bridge.
The monkeys have emerged, their hands soiled with mineral dust, shaking off the spray of water produced by the weight of the mountain they were carrying onto the mountain cascades beside them;
they have reached the forest region where the trees of Nandana grove, brought by the Ten-faced one, provide shade.
Having abandoned the slopes of Suvela, where the forest creepers were bent by the weight of clouds resting heavy with water,
and having crossed the ocean, the monkey host displayed undiminished valor; meanwhile, the world of the Rākṣasas became averse to the tender commands of the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
While the monkey army was occupied with taking up residence on the mountain peaks of Mahodadhi,
Rāma, acting with haste, placed his left hand upon the head of Rāvaṇa— a touch unique in the entire interval between the worlds.
When the sun was split in two by the intervening shadow as it expanded and receded,
the beauty of the earth, together with the goddess Lakṣmī, became radiant;
for Rāma had descended like the moon, whose spot is a mountain, when the affection of the gods was aroused.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Dahamuhavahe* composed by Śrī Pravarasena.
Now begins the ninth chapter:
Then the monkeys behold [Mount Kailāsa], whose great peaks have been increased by the treading of all the world's warriors.
Having brought the southern quarter to an end, Suvela appeared like the world’s destroyer of Madhu (Viṣṇu) after he had traversed the faces of the remaining directions;

or like Śeṣa, the bearer of the world’s burden, when the burden of the earth has been exhausted by the slayer of Madhu; or like the ocean, the lord of rivers, who can bear the weight of the waters that must be discharged.

Capable of supporting the weight of the earth, with mountain torrents flowing like the surging of the ocean, powerful enough to rival the sky, its slopes fit to be obstructed by the winds of cosmic destruction;
it has driven the quarters far away and bent down the entire surface of the netherworld.

The earth’s circumference— with its trees cast far away, with only the fruits and flowers of the nearby trees remaining, with the rivers shifted to the edges, and with the surface of the ocean of the netherworld abandoned—
stands as if it had just been overturned and set upright again by the Boar in his first upheaval.
Its base is filled with water from the underworld; it stands unshakable due to the pressure of the vajra-mouthed [Airāvata] elephant;
its sides are polished smooth by the friction against the shoulders of the celestial elephants like a tethering post;
and even by the king of venomous serpents, who has purified the earth, its root could not be seen.

Even though Hari had increased his strength by seizing the three worlds, he could not lift Mandara, whose lofty peaks were unattainable and which was encircled by the coils of the serpent kings as they writhed around its base; thus, standing nearby, Rāma seized it with his arms like a lion seizing a deer, while the ocean waters were cast aside.
The darkness of the netherworld was destroyed by the light from the base of the jewels struck by the rays of the remaining crest-jewels;
the sky was darkened by the solar orb that had vanished into the narrowness of the unevenly lofty peaks;
and the walls of black stone, polished by contact with the lunar disc, were streaked with lines of nectar.
At night, the celestial river appears with its path marked by the sun’s chariot as it warms unevenly, drenched by the water of moonlight;

with the crescent moon resting upon its ridges, fragments of clouds holding water scattered here and there, and lotus stalks fallen and carried away, it seems like a muddy stream with its heart agitated by the unevenness of the night.
Its mountain peaks, which reveal the paths of rivers and whose distant views are hinted at by the groves of dark forests,
has its slopes of the moon-like [mountain] withered and broken by the wind, causing young shoots to sprout in response;
its summits are raised high aloft, appearing like a vast and manifest image reflected in the waters of the ocean.
Struck by the thunderbolt, it stands like a single severed rope flung upward;
its base is repeatedly obstructed by the hoods of the serpent-king, exhausted from bearing the heavy burden;
and all other mountains have been shattered as they fell upon its lofty peaks, uprooted by the winds of the cosmic dissolution.
Where great buffaloes stand silent and exhausted, driven by clouds that have taken up water;
where clusters of pearls are formed, dried upon stone slabs stained with the blood from the temples of slain elephants;
and where the red hue of fresh sprouts on trees is being washed away by the spray of salt-water waves.
With their ears pricked up as they stood on one leg, having retreated and crouched low out of fear of the lion’s roar,
the mountain caves— filled by the feet of the throngs of rutting elephants that had been driven into them—
seemed to stand on the near side while the quarters of the sky remained fixed upon the far side.
At night, that mountain—with its crest-jewels risen high; with its peaks and summits providing a comfortable resting place for the fragments of the moon;

shaken by the firm arrows of Rāma when he was enraged; shaken by the outpouring from the lunar orb clinging to its peaks; with its base far removed from the reach of the sun’s rays; and with its summit appearing as it vanished beyond the solar orb—[remains].
The uncooked rice for the half-eighth [offering] is like the water of the ocean; likewise, on the surface of the sky,
there is a mass of fragrant smoke arising from the friction of sandalwood trees shaken by the wind,
while the peaks are embraced by the waters of the remaining half-moon, heavy with the ocean being slightly drunk.

Its roar is struck back by the mountain slopes; its mass of lion-like spray is scattered by the upward-thrusting waterfalls; it is joined with the garland of stars and united with the lunar orb resting upon its peaks;
it spreads out before the moon, flowing as an unceasing stream through the caves.
It is a place where lions sleep comfortably on jeweled slabs, where they rest happily seated upon golden rocks;
where tigers, having seized the frontal globes of elephants, toss them aside and turn away;
and where the luster of the gems from the hoods of serpents sleeping in caves issues forth like streams of water.
It bears upon its head— resting on the pearls clinging to the sky— a mane of gems whose tips are difficult to measure, resembling the peaks of the ocean of bones; from it issues forth a lion,
like a cloud cleansed by rain and released from its bonds.

The forest regions, where the white rays of the moon are stirred by the wind and scattered like clouds at the end of an eon, are submerged in the waters of the ocean; there, the rivers flow with their crystal-clear currents turned upward,
carrying trees that lean precariously on their banks, half-submerged yet still lush, and heavy with blossoms.
It carries the mouths of the sun’s chariot horses, which are being shaken by the mountain peaks and waterfalls tossed by the wind;
their reins are slightly slackened, and their mouths are filled with fragments of foam from their saliva,
while they bear the long peaks upon which the blazing light of medicinal herbs shines.
The moon, with its manifest stain of pride, like collyrium applied to its breast during the nights;
the ocean, which uprooted the broad earth and was deeply embraced by the heart of the Primeval Boar,
now filling its river-mouths and drying up the abode of the sea-monsters through the heat of the fire at the end of the aeon.
On this day of the arrival of the unknown, the roar of the elephant-king— filling the caves, causing me to turn back in fear at the echoes ahead, and rending the forest trees— is heard;
it is as red as a lotus in its intensity, and like the sweet warbling of birds heard in lakes.

Carried away by the wind of the tide that has seized the flesh of the deer, with the forests greened by the roar of lions, meeting the edge of the ocean, the circle of the sky revealed, the ten directions pervaded, the sun having risen and set, it flows like a cave through the expanse of the world.
With its waters overflowing from the surging ocean and being carried forward as they gradually recede,

flowing with a sweetness at first yet salty before it; with its peaks shedding forth streams of nectar that shimmer with the luster of jewels, and being tossed by the wide hoods of Śeṣa as he coils around it.

The jewel-peaks, like lakes whose lotuses have blossomed, where the sun’s chariot is caught by the creepers of the mountain ridges, appearing blue as the sky, and emitting rays that spread toward the sides like arrows discharged on the path of the heat-afflicted buffalo to slake its thirst;

The jewel-peaks, like lakes whose lotuses have blossomed, where the sun’s chariot is caught by the creepers of the mountain ridges, appearing blue as the sky, and emitting rays that spread toward the sides like arrows discharged on the path of the heat-afflicted buffalo to slake its thirst.

A forest of *gaa-malia* and *tamāla* trees, with its mountain peaks split by the upraised tails of lions; possessing black rocks struck by buffaloes; where the anger of wild elephants was released against their appropriate stations; and where the pearls from the frontal globes of elephants were shattered by the soles of the paws of lions.
It was a place where herds of deer, fleeing in terror from forest fires, had trampled the confluence of rivers;
where the sun’s chariot turned at its setting; where the stars shone intensely, reflected in the rows of trees on the banks;
and which, even above one seated in repose, seemed to be listening like a second world.
With its sun’s rays half-cut off and the full splendor of all the moonbeams incomplete,
bearing its severed ridges, with peaks sought by Garuḍas as they swoop up and turn back,
it is like a treasury of jewels fashioned from the ocean— the very essence of the nectar of love residing in the hearts of the wives of the gods.

The sweet nectar-juice produced from the hollows of the lotus stalks, the overflowing honey-essence from the groves of *vaula* trees, the deer rendered forgetful by the application of yellow myrobalan paste cooled by intense heat,
and the mountain rocks being licked by buffaloes thirsty for the salty spray of the ocean’s waves.

With its peaks rising high like Mount Raivataka, it possesses the brilliance of pearls formed from the blood of elephants slain by lions; it resounds with the deep, steady, and continuous trumpeting of many young elephants, echoing like the clamor of conchs reflected in the waters of the ocean;
and it is darkened by the pollen of lotuses as radiant as jewels.

Causing the forest to sleep with its essence, causing the lake to sleep with its refuge; having terrified the Rakshasa army, having terrified the unprotected Samudra; destroying the silver of the kingdom, destroying the poison-like splendor.

The sandalwood trees, their trunks encircled by withered and parched medicinal herbs and abandoned by serpents, have their shadows marred and eclipsed by the radiance of the gems on the hoods of venomous snakes hissing nearby;
the ground is whitened by the mass of rays from their jewels, while the sweet warbling of the young female celestial nymphs is heard.

Washed by the waters of the Pālāla river, yet possessing a stainless purity like that of the new moon emerging from a cave; possessing the splendor of a beautiful inner radiance, it is the very essence of the celestial night.
The splendor of the sky, which deceived lions by making them think they were crossing and leaping over swamps;
which satisfied its own weight with clusters of golden sprouts fallen into the depths of lake waters;
and which was beautified by all the dark clouds as if by a girdle formed of the constellations.

Concealing its arms with its peaks, as if concealing its pride; common to the hosts of Asuras while robbing the quarters of their splendor; heroic in dispelling darkness, yet possessing a crest-jewel that rivals the sun.
At the time when Hari was seizing the earth from Bali, while the oceans were being exhausted by the waters,
he remained filling the universe with his body; bearing his natural luster,
with the rays of light from his navel emerging through the openings of his armor like upward-pointing mango blossoms.

The ocean endures the heavy blows of the waves, which have shattered its ridges as if by the heat of the submarine fire; it suffers for the sake of the rivers whose lineages are never severed, like a sun that has lost its orb after passing through a forest fire near its peak.
Upon the nights, bearing the reflection of the young moon’s splendor cast upon the surfaces of individual emerald stone-slabs,
[the mountain] stands like the hoof-prints of the horses of the moon, left by them as they traversed uneven ground while their hooves were stuck in the thickets of tangled creepers.

Surrounded by golden stone terraces like severed moon-discs, bearing forests whose shadows spread upward before the sun has reached them, with serpents resting upon their peaks out of fear of the heat.
Carrying on their temples, which were high enough to suffice for the vast expanse of their faces, the marks of the broad girths [of the goads],
and adorned with pairs of ivory tusks like polished slabs,
the celestial elephants bore the crimson hue of sprouts withered by the heat of their trunks.
The palace, with its tawny walls streaked by the swaying of door-bolts, bearing the branches of *pāriyātra* trees long grown and now released, its splendor whitened by the rays of jeweled bracelets,
resembles the moon whose orb is encircled by the spray of a great waterfall cascading down its slope.
The forest groves of the ocean, bearing flowers washed by the spray of the waves, with their upper parts appearing withered by the sun, darkened as if by the proximity of the sky,
and carrying bees that have returned from the distant paths of the heavens following the celestial chariots.

On the paths of the forest, where the origins of birds have vanished due to the onset of dawn, the darkness is thinning; carrying forth rays that have only slightly emerged, these paths seem pregnant with the fire [of the sun] and bear the marks of the places where the sprouts of jewels have just now been crossed over.
Where the trees have been bent down, where the heaps of rocks are overturned and shattered,

where the fragrance of wild elephants fighting lingers, and where the splinters of teeth fallen from blows still lie upon the broad jeweled slabs that were once tossed up by the strike of Mount Mandara— even today.
The mass of Rāvaṇa’s arrows— whose flow was like the drying up of the ocean's waters, which had not yet lost their innate luster,
which were still clinging to the agitation of the sea, and which were carrying along a multitude of shattered vessels—
stood there like a flock of birds whose wings had been severed by the tip of a thunderbolt.
The lion’s mane was disheveled by the trunk of an elephant that had fallen into a cluster of jars;

the forest flowers were turned upward by bees swerving at the sound of the female deer crying out; and a cool breeze was blowing, fragrant with the scent of blossoms shed from the trees by the touch of the dewy season.
[He] bears [the water] which is broken by the showers of rain, whose waters are slightly moistened, which flows from moonstones,
in which fragrance is scattered unevenly, where the reflection of the water trembles upon the lotus leaves,
and which has its dark-blue essence purified upon the emerald slabs.
At the beginning of the day, she seems to ascend on a horse whose hooves are raised high in a circular gallop; at the end of the day, she seems to descend as the sun passes through its even course.
Where the stars appear at night, they seem to be wandering about, avoiding the uneven terrain.
In the valleys, where the forest-dwellers call out to one another with voices as clear as stars rising in the east,

the moon’s orb— meeting the mountain peaks and struck by the upturned hands of the Cīna women who have been separated from their lovers, as they offer handfuls of flowers moistened by their tears— is scattered abroad.

Like the surface of the sky adorned with planets, it possesses celestial chariots; its peaks obstruct the force of the winds of the cosmic dissolution; it is darkened by clouds through the emergence of rays from its jeweled summits; and in its mountain caves, there is the roar of lions like thick clouds—in which [mountain] the quarters appear as if complete, the earth as if diminished, and the sky as if its end has been reached.
Like an ocean whose waters have subsided, like the netherworld that has vanished, or like the world itself come to rest—
upon whose peaks the horses of the sun turn repeatedly,
their shoulders swaying as they wheel about, their nostrils flared with fear and their chowries tossing as they turn.

In those regions, where at night the forest groves— where the stars have been gathered like heaps of flowers by the bearers of the constellations, and which are as if their first fruits have been taken away— are seen with their stars severed by the day; and where the sighs of lovers, soft as water-lilies, dispel sleep during the nights.

Where the forest buffaloes are drenched by cascades of water from moonstones manifested at the new moon, and where the orb of the moon— its mass of radiance vanished upon being struck by the gems on the necks of lordly serpents— turns back after falling from the peaks and is caught against the uneven slopes of rocky walls.
The ocean, whose depths are revealed as it is tossed about by the trembling and sinking caused by his [the elephant's] trunk,
casts up the surface of the earth with its remaining waters lashed by the wind; therein wander clouds drawn near to the tips of his tusks, which are like the prongs of Indra’s goad.

Where the female elephants, having bathed in the mountain torrents and finding relief from their heat, rest upon sandalwood trees whose branches are shaken by lions— lions whose manes are slightly singed and shaken by lightning-bolts fallen from the sky—
and who, wearying again under the midday sun, are cooled as they sit with their young ones trumpeting.

Where the dust raised by the horses of the chariots— swarming with bees, with the white tails of chowries clinging to the rows of trees, and scattering the pollen of flowers shaken by the moon— is seen darkening their cheeks as it slips down unevenly, greyed by the stain of collyrium.
Where the tears falling from the eyes of the celestial captive women soil the fibers of the kalpa-trees;
where the mountain peak bears the mass of withered and crushed trees,
forever agitated by the coming and going of the sun and moon as they travel through the southern and northern skies.
By which [fragrance],
as it increased, the three worlds seemed to grow— crushing the earth with its weight, filling the netherworld, reaching up to the sky, and scattering in all directions;
there, bees drawn by the scent dwell together with the gods who follow them.
Where the sun, appearing like a celestial elephant, is seen struggling against the night for a single pillar— the sky— mutually opposed;
where, terrified by the imminent presence of Rāvaṇa, his orb of light is caught between the peaks as he seeks an escape through the mountain clefts.

Where, in the lakes whose waters are resonant with the cries of kalahamsas perched upon their banks, the herds of elephants— angered by the calls of those kalahamsas— break out into combat; and where, refreshed by the enchanting songs of kinnaras, the deer close their eyes in sleep and chew their cud so long that their hair stands on end only after a great while.

Where, even at the sight of the sun’s rays, the petals of the clusters of *kumuda* lilies clinging to the vault of heaven do not close; and where, as the moon rises, Ananta spreads his vast mass of hoods, which, illuminated by the radiance of the emerging jewels, supports the heavy burden of the earth.
There is seen a mountain-clinging moon, whose fierce luster resembles a cave, with its rays spreading below and its orb broken by peaks and waterfalls; there,
all three— [the mountain, the moon, and the sky]— are simultaneously present without interval, their forms appearing formidable at the center.
Where the thickets of *thoruṇṇae* creepers stand like golden armlets upon the arms of the world-orbs;
where the moon-stone trees, cool with the pleasure of the new forest-glories, serve as the chariots of night;
and where the paths of the stars, slender as the intervals between forests, are barely discernible.
Where the wind scatters the fragrant young shoots of the *tamāla* tree— unattached to scent, crushed upon the rocky surfaces by the wives of the gods, and drying with their sweet aroma—
and where those shoots, tossed by the wind, repeatedly cling once more to the sky as they rest within the caves.
The rivers, their torrential flows momentarily sweetened by the water drawn upstream against the current,
have their lions swoon and rise again as they fall upon the banks, struck by the impact of the elephants' trunks thrusting against them.

And on the slopes of whose dark jewel-like mountain peaks— resounding with the high-pitched spray of waterfalls and where pairs of *kiṃnara*s fall entangled with one another, startled by the roar of the tiger—
the passion of the celestial wives who dwell there has never known relaxation.

In this great poem (*mahākāvya*) titled *The Slaying of the Ten-faced One* (*Daśamukhavadha*), composed by Śrī Pravarasena, the ninth canto, "The Description of Suvela," and the tenth canto are concluded.
Now, upon the peaks of Mount Suvela, which stand out as if they were his own mountain-foreheads, [the army] dwells with manifest confidence.
The army of monkeys remained settled on the slopes of Mount Suvela—
neither crushed by the Ten-faced one whether he was awake or asleep, nor trampled by the King,
nor overwhelmed by the wind, nor seized by the gods, nor even harassed by the monkeys themselves.
"Is it a river-city? he asked with anger; "The daughter of Janaka lives here," he said with joy.
Thus, as his gaze was cast toward Laṅkā, swayed by the surge of emotion, the Lord’s indignation grew upon hearing of the arrival of his son Rāma, while the mountain peak rose up like a monkey.
Daśagrīva trembled along with Suvela, his fortitude melting away like a flower; meanwhile,
the day, its speech silenced as its attendants dispersed out of fear for Daśagrīva who was distressed by the roar of the monkey host standing nearby,
departed.

As the king, who resembles the sun, draws back his lotus-like day-long splendor, his mass of rays— tawny like yellow orpiment and reddened by the glow of the lotuses— turns away, its outstretched brilliance fading as it touches those who are weary.
The moon’s orb appears as the twilight fades, its thinness revealed by the shadows of the trees;
it possesses the hue of coral and the luster of the temples of elephants smeared with vermilion,
resembling the circle of the sky marked by the mineral-streaks of Mount Mandara.

The quarters of the sky are closing in, darkening the expanse of the earth with their shadows; the day remains but as a fragment, like a mountain peak with its slender rays clinging to it, while the sun,
having reached the slope of the western mountain, sets like a celestial chariot upon the earth’s waist.
The solar disc is seen spreading out like a mountain peak whose minerals have crumbled at the end of the day; as the lotuses close their petals, weary from the fading of their luster,
they scatter drops of honey-essence from their wings, fluttering in the intoxication of the bees.
Both appear alike: the monkeys, whose feet have trampled the earth and crushed the sun;
and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, whose splendor has vanished as his destruction nears, like the sun half-set with only its upper rim remaining visible.
In the sky, the day— its surface parched and dried up—
is withering away day by day like a forest-fire.
The mass of the sun’s rays appears formidable and fierce, like the uprooted base of a tree that has been struck down from behind by a forest-dweller.
But now, at the twilight hour, the orb of the sun has sunk into the mire of its own blood—
the mass of Rāvaṇa’s first head— as it were;
heavy with the red juice trickling from its ripened filaments and weighed down by the burden of bees.
Even the lotus petals, though meeting with the absence of the sun, become formidable; the mass of long rays spreading toward the western quarter appears like a dense darkness,
resembling the path for dragging out the day cast from the mouth of Time.
When the sun has descended to the earth as if by a cord with its orb turned upward, the twilight, crimson like a rising lotus,
is seen placed upon the peak of the setting mountain, as yellow as molten gold poured from the summit of Mount Meru.

The lotus grove blooms white and copper-red like the twilight glow— resembling a mass of dust raised by the chariot of the sun as it halts in its swift course, possessing the hue of a lion’s mane smeared with elephant blood,
trembling in the wind, and with filaments reddened by the twilight.

Behold the twilight shadow at the end of the day: its long duration unmanifest, its uneven glow of evening and night barely severed; it has obscured the ten directions and is a mass of darkness not yet fully formed—a likeness to the place of a fire that has been both kindled and extinguished as it emits the smoke of the final embers.

The sky has become like a whirlpool-lake with the sun situated far away; as the remnants of the day's splendor wane, the glow of lamps emerges, their secondary luster formed by the darkness that has only slightly begun to grow, appearing like the twilight-red still lingering there.
The pair of cakravāka birds— whose bonds of royal constraint were loosened, who found the joy of love through their meeting glances as they stood on the opposite banks,
and whose lives had been drawn out by their cries—
were suddenly severed, while the sky, dark as a tamāla tree, was still thick with the glow of twilight like a golden bracelet.
Having dispelled that darkness, it now stands like the hoof-mark of a celestial elephant upon the mire of the heart;
thin in the near vicinity, thick in the intermediate space, dense in the distance, and though situated equally everywhere, the gloom is seen with its range of vision obstructed.

The trees are barely recognizable by the delight of their flowers— the darkness residing in their dense thickets, the tender young shoots turning dark as they are smeared with gloom, and the blossoms resting upon those shoots—
while their sight has vanished even toward nearby objects, as all directions have been brought together in confusion.
The mass of darkness has become like ground to be ploughed by the sun’s rays;
it spreads forth as a solid block to be shattered, a dense cloud to be lifted up,
a fit object to be suspended by the moon, and a compact heap to be pierced through.
The mass of darkness appears as if filled with the surface of the earth, as if pushing from behind, as if holding in front,
as if pressing from the side, and as if weighing heavily when situated above;
it is seen mingled with gloom, white like a spray of water broken by dark rocks.

With its face half-concealed and its body thinned by the intervening space, the moonlight appears like a pair of scales. The eastern quarter, where the moonbeams have overcome the darkness of the earth’s surface,
resembles an ocean being consumed by a fire of rising smoke.
But now the eastern quarter has become free of darkness, its view unobstructed by the thick mass of moonlight spilling from the rising mountain;
it is made bright by the young crescent moon and resembles a fresh cluster of lotuses with filaments dripping with pollen.
The moon’s orb has not yet completely dispelled the darkness that was close at hand; rather,
having become joined with the peak of the western mountain, it has acquired a white radiance that wipes away the gloom—
a lunar disc made circular by the bite of the tusks of the celestial elephant standing here before it.
But now the expanse of the sky has become like a stone slab strewn with many flowers— the mass of stars appearing turbid as the darkness is dispelled and scattered by the rays of the moon;
it is illuminated by the flickering glimmers of the darkness being shaken off by the rays of the moon that have slightly emerged.
The trees have their slender trunks and branches withered, and their circles of foliage are but slightly bound together;
the orb of the night-maker (the moon), its strength exhausted by the rays that have scaled the sky, has lost its youthful nature and becomes pale as it grows old.

Having carved out the mass of darkness from the surface of the earth— just as if it were a mountain situated there with its peaks so disposed, its slopes so broad, and its river-courses so straight— the moon, having once again cleared away that thick accumulation of gloom, revealed their true forms.
The moon’s rays pursue [the bees], yet they cannot grasp the shade of the trees;
indeed, the moon causes distress to the cluster of petals that quiver from the rubbing of their faces.
Only the bees, each one desiring nothing else, tear at the essence of the night-lotus.

Has the mass of darkness been squeezed out entirely by the moon with his broad rays as if with hands? Has it vanished, exhausted? Or has it been swallowed whole and digested by the moon? It has become as soft as thick mud, easily grasped by the hand, and its corners of the quarters have crumbled away.
Having endured the mass of darkness, as if the surface of the sky were cleansed by the moonlight,

the forests— where the gloomy days of darkness have been pierced and where the moonbeams fall sparsely through the gaps in the branches— manifest themselves with a slight, pleasant light, like tender young shoots.
The bees, having perfumed the tree blossoms and drunk the ichor flowing from the elephants of the quarters, have now left the lotus groves and are hovering over the beds of night-lotuses; thus,
the moonlight, fallen upon the window, becomes as devoid of luster as the moon itself when it has traveled across the sky.

On the surface of the courtyard paved with black gems, the clusters of shadows from the palace pillars appear like the mass of a mountain range grasping the waters of a lake; as the masses of darkness— white as the moon— are scattered by the lions, those long shadows of feet that have emerged from the mud are seen.

The moon, its orb slightly obscured by the mountain peaks, with rays streaming forth through the lattice-like gaps of the clouds, dispels the darkness of the fissures and shatters the expanse of the shadows;
it clings to the sky like a mass of scattered powder, while the clouds are distinguished by their veiled silken garments.
The moonlight, poured through the lattice windows and mingled with the light of lamps, withers away;

like a lotus whose petals have been slightly closed by the coolness of its ripening and which trembles as its broad petals spread under the weight of being filled with thick moonlight that must now be turned back, it fades.
With their peaks shaken by the wind, their shadows dispersed as their branches bend back,
and encircled by moonbeams, the trees seem to be drenched by the spray of moonlight; their thick shade, like the essence of sandalwood, is pierced by the rays of the house-jewels.
The expanse of the sky appears like a mass of moonlight, uneven as if with hollows and ridges; it has lost its own natural luster,
while the moon,
overflowing with light, seems to have cast out its rays, and the soft stars are no longer discernible.
The white mountain peaks, with their lofty summits protruding and their bases visible upon the earth’s surface,

appear like the lunar disc severed by the moon situated in the midst of the sky; yet the mountain valleys are avoided, for they are filled with the darkness descended from the dense canopy of tree shadows.
He licks the opening, which, filled with a mass of moonlight, is like a fordable pool; thus,
the cakravākī, languid and weary at the edge awakened by Love, gazes out.
At twilight, when the bees have emerged in great numbers from the closing blue lotuses,
the hearts of amorous women— overcome by passion and their longing for Rāma’s arrival increasing their agitation— both perceive and abandon the business of love.

The kiss of the lover does not weary young women, even when their longing has been exhausted, when their pleasure is agitated by the onset of passion, and when the aesthetic flavor is broken and then reconstituted; yet they tremble,
gasp, languish, and on the bed, helpless, they unclench their limbs.
It cannot be discerned whether this troop of amorous women is terrified or overcome by passion;

seeing the forest where the tusks of wild elephants have long since scraped away the traces of their beloveds' chests, the company of young women trembles for a long time, as if recalling the deeds of battle.
The pair of eyes, with pupils turned upward in agitation, reveals a state of martial fury; they are like two jasmine buds closed by intoxication,
their petals crushed by the assault of bees.
Ah, at this evening— devoid of the moon’s radiance, where the joy of longing for a lover increased by intoxication has vanished,

where pride has been uprooted by passion, and where the pleasure of love has been abandoned by the king— the night turns dark; and the woman, tormented and provoked, her shame exhausted, enters the body [of the lover].
And the company of wanton women, their hearts revealed by intoxication and having tasted the pleasure of being kissed, sleeps soundly;
for them, the side-long glances of their lovers— whose lips were reddened by anger and who wept during the forceful kisses of their husbands—
now steal away the weight of their resentment as they speak with faces turned away.
The company of wanton women does not take up their departure, nor do they compose their hair, nor do they ask the female messenger;
struck by the sight of the moonlight, they tremble with bewildered hearts, disregarding the talk of Rāma as the activities of the young women proceed as before.
The arrival of the night, which brings the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, shines among the lords of the night;
yet, having turned away from the presence of their beloveds, how is it that the multitude of women repeatedly turns back even the female messengers who speak falsehoods directly to them?
On their couches, during a lovers’ quarrel, while being teased by their beloveds seated face-to-face,
they could not turn away; yet, though they found a moment’s pleasure through conciliation, their eyes again overflowed with tears as they were tormented by the memory of their resentment.
In the hearts of the young women, anger heavy with long-held resentment gradually subsides;

embarrassed, they touch their lower lips and pull back their girdles; they restrain themselves and speak of delusion; and the company of playful women, distressed by the sight of their beloveds, speaks to their friends.
The going to bed of the playful women— eager to rise,

radiant with the embrace of their lovers, and whose ornaments were yet unfinished— is beautiful, for it is hindered by their friends who, having finally granted them the pleasure [of sleep], restrain them with steady gazes and silent words.
The company of wanton women, their hearts agitated, is known by their lovers to be feigning anger;
they restrain their growing friend, bashfulness, as she increases along with the lover’s persistent pursuit, and it is Love alone who first casts off shame for a long time.

Having been observed by young women with their hands occupied by their companions, their faces marked by slight smiles, the female messenger is addressed with agitation and in a faltering, uneven manner;
yet while she addresses one person in one way before her companions, she speaks quite differently to the messenger.
In the company of young brides, even when their courage is shattered by the pain of the fresh nail-marks,

the young women somehow bring their faces close to the embrace of their lovers at the sight of them; with their faces turned away as they struggle to turn back for a kiss, they somehow utter faltering words and find a steadiness of mind.
With pride abandoned, his heart turned away from passion, and seated before his beloveds with a dense eruption of horripilation,
the assembly of wanton women did not drink even when offered wine; they did not incline their faces, nor did they forcibly press their lips.
In some places, young women who have turned away at their first encounter plead for their lover to take heart, saying, "Let him wait;
he will not come here even though evening has already dawned.
Thus do the female messengers weigh the situation against the assembly of elegant women whose lovers have been brought back by them for the first time.
In the case of the wanton women, both their pleasure and their pain have their true nature revealed;
they speak with confidence like friends, disregarding all shame.
By the light of the moon, intoxication has increased its sway, as if the splendor of the moon itself were augmented by intoxication.
By both of them, indeed, love was driven to its extreme; by love, indeed, both of them were driven to their limit.
At night, by the moon’s rays, and by love, along with the intoxication of wine, the intense passion of young women for their beloveds has ascended far, far away.
This is the tenth chapter; the eleventh chapter is the *Yugmaka*.
When evening had arrived— its moon withdrawn, its onset of night long severed, its cessation of activity brought to a halt,
and the multitude of loving women rendered desolate— the Lord of the Rākṣasas gave way to a long reflection that stirred a heart made firm and steadfast by anxiety.
Having looked simultaneously with his ten mouths at the ten directions which were empty, the Ten-faced One sighs, ponders, groans, wrings his arms, shakes his mass of heads,
and laughs a laugh empty of joy— Rāvaṇa, whose passion has found no outlet in Sītā.
He prizes the forest of Vatsa, which was embraced by his father as he turned back from being carried away;
yet he despises the multitude of words that have not reached the nectar-dew of his beloved’s mouth— words that were broken, turned back, and shattered even as he tried to restrain them.
As her heart trembles with an uneven agitation, it leaps quickly even though she strives for steadiness; thus,
