her face— resting slightly upon her unevenly twisted, sparse, and outstretched fingers—
slips onto her shoulder, while a flood of tears flows from her eyes due to her bursting laughter.
He hears the sound of victory from his beloveds, which is sweet though choked by their gasping and faltering as their lip-wounds smart; he yawns with a heavy heart,
seeks a great bed, longs for the end of night, and loathes the day.
She withdraws and then turns back again; with his heart anxious in its search for a way to win her,
even as he conceals it,
a cool conversation— though rooted in his heart— proceeds equally before the faces of both [women] who stand there.
She gazes at him when he is looked at; she speaks while he speaks; she takes his name; and she stands beside him even when he is thinking of something else.
That flower-cluster, unevenly heaped at the edge of the inner chamber, reveals her very torment to him.
Exhausted by deep sighs, with the sprouts of the celestial tree withering,
he leans upon her broad hips as if weighed down by the burden;
his hands flailing on the uneven ground-bed, his waist deeply indented from being bent far back.
Bestowed with courtesy and affection, his heart yearning for the daughter of Janaka, his face momentarily bewildered, his multitude of faces leaps up among those in his own inner apartments;
he who passes away from one group of wanton women, laughing, free from envy.

His face, which was otherwise marked by unbearable anguish and dejected with sorrow, now bears a subtle smile; though his heart is fixed elsewhere, the Ten-faced One hears the deceptive words concerning the delivery of Sītā and does not clearly perceive that his beloveds have been given away to another.
Heavy with lordliness and envy, his support growing increasingly precarious,
he somehow passes the moment through the amorous woman’s conversation accompanied by embarrassed laughter; meanwhile,
all other activity is suspended as his arms are thrown around her neck and his footsteps falter unevenly.
He is suspected by his wives, who are distraught; clearly, he is not recognized as the one who has addressed them with a slip of the tongue regarding their lineage.

Somehow the Ten-faced One establishes himself—his speech delivered amidst unspoken delusion, his tears falling from the eyes of his beloveds, and himself gazed upon by them in anger with speechless astonishment.
Even though his heart was not pleased, the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) greeted the words of his beloveds with a loud "hum" uttered with unrestrained passion;
while his lips were slightly parted and trembling, he welcomed their ill-advised advice, which they had looked upon him with a gaze of frantic excitement in their intoxication of love.
She laughed at herself as she turned back after having offered her seat without any affection;

he went to such an excess that even when being rebuked by his beloveds, he was neither recognized, nor, having been recognized, was he laughed at, nor, having been laughed at, did he feel remorse, nor did he recover.

And he began to reflect, his eyes fixed upon two [monkeys] who were sitting together, their breaths heavy with sighs spreading from their mouths; while one monkey, having placed its hand on the cheek near its face,
was being tolerated by the host out of fear that it might disturb the peace of night and day.
Whose benefit does he seek? My own heart, which has not yet attained sexual union, yearns for him.

Why do I crush the monkey-force—restless, noisy, and fruitless—which stands nearby in the midst of a sudden attack, having been seized, dragged, struck down, and cast aside by the agitation of my arms flailing through the openings between the trees?
How can Janaka’s daughter— whose face is cast down and rendered speechless by his seizing her hair, and whose waves of tears sway like the world-rolling locks of the moon-beamed Shiva—
be anything but adverse to separation when her husband has approached her? For she is one whose heart is already turned toward him.
Even another [woman] would not desire the moon; how much less would the lotus refuse a request when the sun is seen? Even the Fortune of the Three Worlds could not bribe her;
she does not even consider the destruction of her body. How, I wonder, might she become gracious?
Seated upon her own majesty, having disregarded the courage of all other noble men—
if only Janaka’s daughter were now under my power, she who has seen the head of the slain Rāghava;
for one who has failed to protect those seeking refuge is beyond reproach, as the bonds of hope have been shattered.
Helpless and friendless, the person, out of fear, commits the rash act of violating the established order;
yet, when his face is wrinkled with frowns and yawns of exhaustion, his attendants,
commanded by the knitting of his brows, gather around him on both sides simultaneously.

Even with ten mouths acting together, the Ten-faced One is not able to utter at once that which has been multiplied by his single heart; for the speech, heavy with syllables pregnant with the fulfillment of long-cherished desires,
is begun by one mouth and dropped by another through the grip of joy.
One half was spoken by another mouth, and somehow that [other half] was fashioned by him; then, with sorrow gripped within, as he spoke, he sighed— a sigh that sent smoke flickering from his mouth,
tormented his solitary heart, and faltered through the ten throats of Rāvaṇa.

And she laughed at that illusory creation, whose eyes were fixed motionlessly upon the sight of the enemy as they turned sharply, with her upper body bent by the weight of the third eye situated on the side of her palm-like hand pressed against the earth, and who gave a reply at the very moment of his command.
Then, right there, they fashioned that very head of Rāma— headless, pale from separation from Sītā—
with the surface of its forehead rippling with eyebrows knit together in indignation,
as if it were a severed head brought back to life.
And having set out, the Rākṣasas— stumbling as they rose from their prostrations in agitation,
somehow completing the forest of joy, and busied with executing the command of Daśagrīva as it was fully communicated—
arrived at the lotus-bud formed by the mud of the waters gushing forth from the fissures in the jeweled mountain ridges.

And they behold the forest of *pāmā* creepers, with young shoots emerging from the broken branches of trees shattered by the wind, and with their palms resting upon breasts that have been displaced by faces fixed in sleep.
Her eyes startled by the sound of footsteps, which she suspected to be the arrival of her husband’s enemies;
the knot of her braid loosened because the jeweled hairpin sent by her beloved was missing;
and her breasts languid, their slopes drenched by falling tears as white as washed lime.
Her thick, dark tresses are disheveled; her face is obscured by streaming tears;
her waist is bereft of its girdle; her ornaments cast aside and her beauty withered; her eyes remain motionless and vacant, fixed upon the heart of her beloved who has departed for a short while.
With joy surging like waves of tears at the sound of Kaikeyī’s words,
with the places of tear-drops rendered harsh by the pale-red Vasuka flowers slightly moistened by dew,
and with the luster of her lips settled in their own naturally ashy state after being wiped away;

Bearing a voice emerging from his withered cheeks, like the moon whose digits are incomplete, long, and yet to be fulfilled by the days of the poets— its surface resembling the luster of a slightly opened, curved wound revealed by the glow of his body.
Her bracelets appearing thin upon the path of binding her ornaments, her tremulous eyes visible as she moves, her creeper-like arms quivering with longing to embrace him,
with her lover standing nearby, she seems to languish with passion as if on a single bed.
Her limbs collapsed, exhausted by a longing doubled by the sight of the moon difficult to endure;
her heart motionless, as if its life had been seized and rubbed away by the hand of the night-stalker;
she carries [him] with her hand, which reaches far down, its palm heavy with tears.

Her face, with its single side made manifest by the luster of the gems on her closely pressed fingers, appears as if it were a solitary flank; her heart is turned toward Rāma, whose distress has been dispelled by the embrace of his arms;
and she is distracted, wondering, "What will become of the Ten-faced one? as he lies near, dejected at the approaching battle.

Having seen her—whose heart was distressed by the sight of her beloved, which had been revealed by a collective glance; whose heart was eager for the sight of her beloved, which had been revealed by a half-closed gaze; whose heart was upturned in longing; who was fainting from the sight of her husband’s face as it was turned upward in his own longing; and whose heart was pained, with her duties forgotten as they surged forth—[the messenger]...
Then those Rākṣasas, who were servants to the wives of Māyāmaya and Rāma,
stood before her with Rāghava’s face turned skillfully toward her and his left hand resting upon the middle of the bow.
Upon seeing it, she was despondent; as it was being presented, she began to tremble.
When the jewel-bearers said, "The head of Rāma," Sītā fell into a swoon on the spot, her cheeks pale from the slackening of her grasp and heaving with gasps.
With her left breast pressed against his right, the daughter of Janaka lay with her right breast raised high;
when her kinsmen were dying, who indeed could be their refuge? Thus, swallowed by profound grief, the daughter of the Earth fell to the ground and fainted.
She made no effort to free her arms, nor could she even lift Rāma’s head;
having succumbed to total delusion and being rendered helpless by the loss of life, she sat upon the earth with breath momentarily still, her complexion turned dark by the gloom of fainting.
Her face— with eyes half-closed in fainting, pupils sinking away,
the pain of separation forgotten, and the hope for Rāma’s death momentarily abandoned—
has found only the bliss of being closed by her father’s daughter in a swoon.
In her heart, which was transformed by the hardness of her breasts, not even the slightest [sign] was seen; yet her long,
heavy sighing was indicated only by her trembling lower lip and her indistinct breaths—
thus, even at the cessation of her fainting, she remained collapsed in exhaustion.
Behold the cluster of stars, its pupils heavy with the suffering of being pierced by minute shafts; it appears as if violently severed by the uneven blows of the tips of drawn sword-blades. 4.

With its curved tip darkened by the feathers of an arrow drawn from a distant bow and struck against it; with its opening widened by the flesh of a severed neck, white with flowing blood and quivering; and with a spray of droplets clinging to the edge of the wound where the weapon broke and fell upon impact.

With his fangs slightly visible, set in the root of his lip bitten by sleep; with his dark throat-wound filling with a mass of slushy blood from his own countenance; and with the knitting of his brows and the contraction of his eyebrows lost upon the slope of his forehead due to the grip of the night-stalker’s claws.

With her gaze fixed upon Rāma’s head— lightened by the flow of blood from her throat and with pupils no longer rolling in her heart— she, distressed by the throbbing of her cheeks, dropped her hand to her chest;
yet, deprived of life and motion, she went to the surface of the earth solely by the weight of her breasts.
While she was in a state of swoon, what was this? Simultaneously in the sky and in all directions, her face became lost in a vacant, wandering gaze, uttering delirious lamentations;
and having observed it thus, I remained standing and then sitting, facing in that very direction.
Though she sought his word, she did not find it, and death somehow came upon her; then,
with limbs outstretched, her braid of hair spread across the path filled with dust, Janaka’s daughter fell,
her breasts rolling as they struck the surface of the earth.
Although she was seated with her entire body, the middle part of her— deprived of all appearance of folds through total emaciation and compressed by her breasts and hips— could not reach the ground;
for when her lover’s face, radiant with a sudden glance, was to be seen with longing, it remained suspended in the air.
Having long fallen into a swoon, her heart has now returned along with her tears;
somehow regaining consciousness, she seeks to hide her necklace which clings to her cheeks that are wet with weeping, but her hand, rendered powerless, cannot reach it.

Thrown up by her agitation, the head of Rāma— its descent exhausted, its movement completed— fell upon her lap; yet, unable to look at it directly as it lay upon her bosom before reaching her breasts, she somehow turned her face toward it with a bewildered heart.

With her creeper-like arms bent by the force of words that were exhausted from weeping, Janaka’s daughter began to lament; having cast aside all concern for her own body due to the sorrow for Rāghava,
her breasts— pale with blood flowing from the path of her hands— stood high and heaving.

The mere burden of separation is not such a terrible endurance of suffering as that which you have seen and endured— the final end, terrifying to women, which was fixed in my heart with the thought, "I shall be released upon your chest."
Tell me, for whose sake was she prepared to depart from this earth? Let her sorrow in separation from you be appeased.
"I shall see you"—with such a thought, my life has somehow been sustained by me;
yet now that she is seen by me, even my fulfilled desires do not satisfy me.

"The Fortune of Kingship, fickle toward the distinctions of many men, will become the husband of the Earth; how then is this extraordinary misfortune arisen for me alone? Thus she spoke, and looked with eyes wide with poison.
O Lord, it was because my shame had vanished that your face became clearly visible to me; I wept,
I endured separation from you, and I lived together with the female nāga-spirits as if with my own friends—
yet this life of mine would have perished even now, had I not seen you.
Now that you have gone to the other world, appearing as a mere memory of your resolve,
my heart— though this is a cause for joy— cannot restrain its tears because it has not seen the slaying of the Ten-faced one; even the bond of hope does not hold back my heart.
But even when I reflect upon it, I do not know by whom my life was withheld;
for my sake, you crossed the ocean of love, and even death was accepted by you, O Lord. Yet today, my heart still maintains its ungratefulness.
O Rāma, having grasped you and reckoned your virtues, people will consider you a man of noble intellect and turn away from me, remembering my own waning womanly nature;
but how shall I behold the face of the Ten-necked one, which was once the abode of the ten directions, now struck down by the wound of your arrow? Thus she spoke.
My desires, turned away by great misfortune and directed toward a chasm,
have been frustrated; for even in our separation, which was but slight, people suspected a bond of love between us, yet now, seeing him in such a state, this alone is the fruit for me.
Consoling him sweetly with her face turned upward toward her hand—him who was motionless with distress and whose pair of eyes were vacant as his heart failed—Taraṅgavati says to him:
"His sorrow has not yet vanished; the simple girl has not yet seen true love, for she has not yet been broken."
A fool accompanied by young women imagines fear of the sun even from darkness;
why do you, knowing him to be one who has consumed the root of the three worlds and who bore the burden of battle released by the treacherous Mahinda, compare your husband to ordinary men?
The earth— whose waters are the Amīlya ocean, whose great mountains stand unshaken, and whose ridges are not uneven—
how does she bear your head, severed and fallen,
which has its branches broken by the wind and its lotuses closed by the touch of the moonbeams?
"How can it be that the grove of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa’s palace has become a forest for the destruction of Rāma?
Do not weep; wipe away your tears. Having turned your face toward your shoulder and recalled the pain of separation, you shall weep again in the lap of your husband."

O Airāvatī, you shall behold the son of Daśaratha— his pale complexion withered by separation from you, beautiful to look upon now that his anger has subsided, his bow laid aside and at peace, yet filled with indignation—
slain by Hara in a throat-cutting strike that even he would not have desired.
If even the head of Rāma— though severed, still grasped by the hand, and being struck— were to come into contact with you,

why do you falter while beholding the Pampa forest, which provides such cause for consolation and where the trees are tossed about by the mountain torrents sent forth at Rāma’s command, shattering the pride of the Ten-faced One?
How does he, whose world of gods has been destroyed and who holds up the universe with his arms alone— yet now finds the night-ranger’s sleep falling upon him—
sustain himself for even a moment without you? Thus have you fallen into a swoon, your limbs exhausted and despondent, collapsed in a faint.
Knowing clearly that this is the work of a Rākṣasa, I too am despondent;

yet even now, before the assembled night-stalkers, why do you not seize Rāghava, who has been driven from the path fashioned between Mount Suvela and Mount Malaya and pushed onto the peak of Mount Trikuṭa?
O you with hips like Mount Malaya, having wandered upon the dry land and dwelt upon the peak of Mount Suvela in the waters of the great ocean— why do you still harbor resentment toward Rāvaṇa?
Therefore, you who have failed to follow my advice, your life is now departing as you are being tormented.
O dear Trijatā, daughter of Janaka, seated upon my chest in a manner befitting the affection of a friend,
as she leans to one side, her tears—
rising from the pressure of being pressed against my cheek and clinging to the corners of her eyes— have fallen.
She began to speak again, rising from her seat and gasping for breath;
with her braid swaying against her chest and the dust of the earth clinging to her face and breasts, that daughter of Janaka said:
"Tell me, it was only after seeing him first that I sat down upon this ground."
I see him again, as if emerging from delusion, and I hold onto my life;
O friend, I have seen such an end for you, my lord, in the abode of the Rākṣasa.
Yet even today, though struck by infamy, my heart smokes but does not burn.

This deed you have done is like that of a demon, not like that of a man; O Lord of the Niṣādas, why did it not occur to you that for me, who was easily reached as soon as thought of, death would not be like that of a woman?
For me, who came here swiftly at the command of the Wind-god, [your act] has become a support for my life.

O Rāghava, though my life was made light by separation, I have lived on; with my face veiled, my braid loosened as I turned toward you, my heart overcome by fainting, I sat down once more, sighing weakly and speaking but little.
With her hair disheveled and unevenly scattered as the knot of her braid was loosened and broken,
she fell upon the surface of the earth with a heart despairing of the couch of peacock feathers; there,
with a hand reddened and trembling from the blow, she covered her face as if with a fresh sprout.
I could not wipe away [the tears], for they had settled upon one of her cheeks;
when my gaze, distressed by weeping, could not somehow catch even her face as it was turned toward me, then, with great effort, I somehow pressed my palms against her eyes.
With tears shed from her eyelashes due to the uneven gusts of the wandering wind, she gazes at the face of Rāghava as it rolls upon the surface of the earth, trampled by the night-stalker;
her eyes, fixed motionless and upturned, reveal her overwhelming sorrow.
Her gaze, fixed upon Rāma’s head, is washed away by tears and cannot be restrained;
seeing him, her heart is once more filled with the singular sentiment of death.
With her eyes turned toward Trijaṭā, she makes a piteous smile, saying, "Farewell to me," as her vision is lost amidst a torrent of tears.
In this separation from Rāma, which my cruel heart has accepted as a state of woe, endure this shameless death of mine, lightened by my lack of affection for you; weep,
for this is the fate of everyone, but it is not the end for those who possess honor.

Saying "It is worthy of you," she fell down after striking her firm, heavy breasts; yet even as she lamented with a voice soft and exhausted by grief, Sītā could not bring herself to call out "O son of Daśaratha" or "My dear," out of shame for her life.
She does not wish to ask for forgiveness, nor does she let her arm fall upon his body as if it were that of a stranger;
she sheds tears but does not restrain them, for her heart has gained the conviction that she must die—
such is the plight of Yaugandharāyaṇī.
To him, whose heart was not turning away from the thought of death, Trijaṭā proceeded to speak;
with her limbs supported by her trembling hands as she leaned forward, she said these words of affection:
"O Queen of the Night, do not despise my speech."
In the garden and in the forest, you gather the fragrant blossoms of the creepers;
why then, my friend, do you live on? If the death of Rāghava were not a lie, O friend, then your heart would be distressed by the grief of dying for the sake of the Lord of the Raghus.
But since he lives, your heart suffers in vain, tormented by the thought of your own death.
Even to think of it is impossible; yet, if this were as you imagine it to be, then why would my consolation now toward you be appropriate for anyone?
For the entire city of the night-stalkers has been emptied of its cries of lamentation, just like a house during a round of mourning.
By what poet will the lineage of Raghu be rendered free of Rākṣasas?
Rāma is not being subdued; the three worlds shall soon be without Rākṣasas.
I say this clearly: believe it, for to whom is the destruction of one's own kin dear?
Arise, abandon your grief; wipe this breast-surface soiled by tears. Listen, bird: shedding tears at the onset of battle is not fitting for a husband;
save for the Lord of the Raghus, whose face is marked by drops of perspiration born of shame.
By whom else has the ten-faced Rāvaṇa been rendered instantly devoid of luster, obstructed at his feet?
Before long, that son of Raghu shall loosen your braid— its dark lashes trembling as they are grasped by his hand,
its uneven mass tossed up by fingers quivering with emotion.
I do not grieve so much for you as I do for the nature of the Ten-faced one, which has been overturned— [a nature] that was rendered light by a lack of shame, yet which,
while maintaining its status as the Lord of the Raghus, displayed its true strength in the slaying of Vālin, and provided a dry land-path across the ocean by piercing it with arrows.
Behold the lightness of Rāvaṇa’s arm, which could not lift the golden Lanka-gate!

You have been seen by me in a dream, your face beautiful as a reflection of the moon and sun, with the white silk of the celestial elephant’s ear fluttering against your uplifted shoulders, covering half your face.

I have seen the Ten-faced one, the path of whose ten mouths was revealed by the dragging [of his victims], and whose mass of faces was faltering as they were partially joined together after being pulled apart by the firm noose of Death.
Therefore, take heart; let this inauspiciousness perish now while I—
Let this illusion— lightened by its perceived ultimate truth and disregarded as fruitless—
now turn back, were it not for the hope that even Rāma’s head, though in such a state, might still breathe and, like nectar, taste the joy of your touch.

Her heart tormented by the unbearable blow of the thunderbolt of Rama’s love being proclaimed, she remembered him and wept with a choked voice, uttering cries of "Ah me!"— though she was accustomed to death,
she could not be comforted even by Tāṭakā’s words until the roar of the mountain [Hanumān] reached her ears.
The deep drum of victory, sounding the auspicious battle-call for Rāghava, was not heard; instead,
she sighed— a sigh whose object was her departed grief, which bound her hope for life with various consolations, and whose full breasts were raised high.
When she had been consoled and made happy, when she was reassured by his repeated declarations of truth,
and when her fear of separation had vanished, the pain of parting once again gathered in her heart as the delusion of her deceit departed— at the sound of the monkeys’ preparations for battle.
The fruit of the speech born of affection and love for Tiaḍā has been seen by Jaṇaa’s daughter. Thus ends the eleventh act; the twelfth act is concluded.
Then the dawn arrived, its hue like the deep red of the rising sun, with the swarms of kalahamsas becoming soiled by the pollen falling from the slightly opened blue lotuses,
the groves of night-lotuses slightly closed and turning pale green, and its base obscured by the moonlight as if by the turbidity of fresh water.
The western quarter of the night recedes like a bank washed away by the stain of the mineral ores [of dawn];
on the surface of the earth, as the moonlight is struck by the rays of the dawn, the form of the tree-shadows is discerned, grey and distorted as they merely flicker.

The lotus grove closes; the lunar orb has half-set and its radiance has faded; the night’s splendor dissolves; and the eastern quarter appears, its fresh stars reddened by the dawn, like a young mango tree with sprouts darkened by the dust of nocturnal gloom.
The moon has now reached the western slope of the sky, which is as rugged as a mountain peak with jagged slabs of black stone;
its surface is turbid with the hue of the hooves of elephants drenched in fresh water, and it appears as if it were falling from the heavens, tilted by the rising dawn.
The forests have become breezy, filled with the clear and sweet cries of birds emerging from their nests and the humming of bees; their young shoots are lightened by the shaken resin.
The moonlight, though thinned by the touch of dawn, remains dense as it follows its own lunar orb.
Having fallen from the peaks of the mountain, the orb of the moon— supported by outstretched hands—
somehow passes the night’s sorrow of separation from its beloved; then,
at dawn, it follows the cakravāka bird, calling out in response as if to rise up for it like a female companion.
The moon has arisen, its orb made formidable by the rays of the medicinal herbs clinging to it;
from its summit flows a stream of moonstones set in motion by the other moon;
the constellations are deeply bowed down, and its moonlight falls away as it is struck by the tips of the dawn’s rays.
The night has become fruitful through the pleasure of union with her beloved; it falls as if intoxicated, while the moon rises again from the mountain peaks.
Dawn arrives, weary of the longing for separation brought by the night, yet the god of love remains undaunted. The surface of the sky seems to fall, and then rise once more.
Its passion increased by confidence, its tongue remaining after the stumble of the night,
skillful through the dissolution of pride, the dawn-light is more intense than the evening; its redness transferred to the lips, it is supported by a lotus placed there by a little wine.

In the house, the fragrance released by amorous women does not fade; the cluster of loosened hair, the hips obstructed by twisted girdles, and the slender forms abandoned by their lovers—all bear the lingering scent of their beauty.
The entire assembly of graceful ladies remains permeated with the perfume that clings to them.
With their left feet poorly placed, their heavy thighs swaying as they stumble unevenly,
and their faces smeared with the dust of the evening sun like the mud of a lotus pond agitated by them, young women proceed with difficulty toward their beloveds and turn back again.
Like a deer that has strayed from its place, having wandered about at night and returned, the day-damsel, awakened by the dawn, raises her foot as if to drive away the approaching sun,
while her lotuses scatter their petals.

Each individual [lotus] is severed from its stalk, and as the moon’s reflection— disturbed by the agitation of the ocean waters— clings to its mother like a child, the multitude of conchs becomes the refuge for the beds of lotuses that are rising up after their long suppression.

The scent, though stirred by the wind and sweet as honey, remains rich and full; that very same fragrance which was a support for the eyes of the host of lovers as they shed tears, has now become the final joy of the embrace for the Rākṣasa warriors.

Then Rāvaṇa, whose happiness was interrupted by the thought of battle, for whom the day of avenging his enmity with the Ten-faced one had arrived, and who had found an opportunity for wrath, woke up without having obtained sleep,
enduring the pain of separation from Sītā for only the duration of four watches.
A long time has passed, yet for the Lord of the Raghus, that single night was not even one *samā*.

His gaze— slipping from the corners of his eyes, which were reddened by the remnants of sleep, and weighted down by the heavy burden of his bowstring— remained fixed upon his bow as he stood in the midst of battle.
Behold this couch of stone, fragrant with fading flowers, its surface stained by the dust of her sighs, uneven from her constant tossing, and betraying the anguish of her heart.
Having long congratulated his left arm— which was as heavy as a diamond and which portended an imminent reunion with his beloved— he,
who honors righteousness at every moment, drew back and fixed an arrow along the path of the bowstring.
Having bound her mass of matted hair— fragrant with the tamāla paste rubbed and applied upon it—
and having offered a pair of garments, she whose tears had long since ceased, yet whose face was still flushed with anger suppressed for so long, [departed].

He takes up his bow, its string drawn tight and difficult to behold due to the star-like pupils of his eyes fixed on Lanka; its tip is repeatedly placed upon the path of the couch made empty by Sita, while his face is turned upward in deep longing for her during their separation.

Having made ready that opponent who was stationed upon the surface of the earth, firmly grasped by the pressure of his left hand, and bent by the weight of his body as he turned with his right hand— [the hero] addressed him with a sigh, slow and heavy, shaking his head.
The Lord of the Raghus set forth, his only equipment being a bow fashioned from a mountain he had torn asunder; and the monkey army followed,
with its peaks touching mountains of equal size as they moved,
their trees recognizable by their branches resting upon corresponding arms.
The wicked are emboldened; what can they achieve with the weight of their armor?

For poets, their own strength alone is the shield, their unimpeded arms are the weapon—a weapon awakened by the course of battle, refined by illusion, and possessing the essence of the lords of the night.
Distressed by the thought, "How can Viśvaṇa’s army—skilled in the paths of Laṅkā and already prepared for battle—be abandoned while it stands at the vanguard?
Sugrīva grieves; and Rāma, having taken up his weapons, grieves for the race of the night-stalkers along with Viśvaṇa.
When the bow was drawn by Rāghava, who agitated the mountains and stirred the ocean,

Laṅkā trembled as if its houses and ramparts were being shaken; with her limbs covered in horripilation and her face lit up by unprecedented joy, the daughter of Janaka appeared like one whose body was trembling from the unevenness of her own movements.

Having heard the sound of the bow, which was like Rāvaṇa’s first address, the young women fainted; and the clamor of the monkeys, pleasing to the ears of Sītā, bewilders the city folk like a thunderbolt strike upon the mountain-like hearts of the lord of the Rākṣasas.

Having crossed the ocean whose waters were stirred by the agitation of the best of monkeys and cleansed of its impurities, the mountain, with its cavernous mouth filling with water, roars with a subsiding resonance,
having subdued all other clamor— the sound of his bowstring twanging as it was first struck.
Having been informed by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, whose face was agitated with indignation and wonder,
the Lord of the Rākṣasas finally became calm; disregarding the monkey host that had crossed the ocean and was exulting in battle, he awoke from his own sleep-testing dream.

Then the Ten-Faced One (Rāvaṇa) bore a sleepless slumber, finding pleasure only in turning over during the second watch; it was a sleep accompanied by the auspicious sounds of unevenly uttered prayers and interrupted by the lamentations of his wives,
while his eyes remained heavy with sleep, dark and sluggish as if intoxicated by honey.

Having turned them back onto the lap of his own couch, he releases his pair of arms— which, marked by the scars of bow-strings and filled with the remnants of sleep, have their fingers formidable as they leap one over another like high jeweled arches— and which belong to the Ten-faced One.
Then,
the Rākṣasas, having risen for the alarm of battle and seized their respective weapons, prepared to strike the ten-headed Rāvaṇa’s war-trumpet—
which betokens the equipment for combat and causes a great agitation among the gods by its shaking the pillars as it resounds with fear.

Having taken a small amount [of wine] clinging to their throats as they closed their eyes, and having been grasped by young women who were bidding them farewell, the lower lips of the lovers— whose grip remained loose and unrelaxed— are being led away from the single battlefield of sleep by the faces of those women.

When the sound of the battle preparations is heard, the women’s arms— clinging to the necks of their lovers— are slightly lowered; their fear melts away due to the exhaustion of lovemaking, and they quickly take up their weapons with hands that are clumsy from being turned back by the embrace.

The night-stalkers (demons) toss about; though the young women resist the embrace of their lovers— which brings the pleasure of a lover's hug as their breasts heave like calves— once the beloved has committed an offense and shattered their pride, that long-nourished indignation no longer takes root in hearts already overwhelmed by fear.
The more her beloved restrains her— her heart swelling with indignation at the slight she perceives from her husband—
the more Bhairava’s martial ardor increases through his honored jealousy; though held back by her husband’s hands and faltering in her resolve, her heart remains dyed with love.

Held back by pride yet driven out by the fury of battle, the night-stalkers (rākṣasas) long for the joy of combat with the gods; they feel ashamed when the burden of war is lightened by the heads of monkeys, and they cannot endure the onset of their enemy’s sword-blades.
Terrorizing in the forest openings, resonant amidst the forest thickets, stumbling and falling, uneven upon the surface of his chest, and resting against his bare back— this makara-hide armor,
whose strength was witnessed in the battle of the gods, serves as the moving bridge for the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
With his hand skillfully released from the arrow, he tightened his girdle in excitement; as he prepared himself,
the armor— stretched wide across his many-jointed necks— slipped loosely down over his chest,
which was made slender by his hand raised to his face.
As he stirs the great ocean, which has been made heavy by the earth he has bestowed upon it, his own armor, piled upon his chest, shifts under its weight;
and from it emerges a luster as smooth as a polished surface, visible through the pestle-like tusks of Rāvaṇa.
The formidable armor of the one-eyed Indra is now being raised upon his chest;
because of that armor, the long,
dangling girdle resting upon his thighs has become separated from the luster of his body, making the sky appear as if its dark clouds have vanished.

The war-elephant is distressed; having fastened his armor— its straps severed by the tips of thunderbolts and its shoulder-hair exposed and turned upward on the chest— he stands with eyes rolling in rage at the mass of wounds from the fire-weapon, which have long since healed and burst open again.
Blood flows for a long time from the cavities of his wounds like that from a storm-cloud;
on the chest of Nīumbha, who is trembling with the force of indignation,
the *māḍhī*— its seams clearly revealed— is bursting open like a loosened iron chain.
Even his son fastens on armor well-tested to withstand the blows of the gods' weapons;
yet he does not place before him that which is difficult to ward off due to the irresistible arrows of Rāma,
nor that which bears the mark of being pierced by the embraces of a lover who has turned away in haste.
Sāraṇa himself does not fasten his armor, as he wipes away the fragrance from [Kumbha’s] breasts;

for it is fitting that Kumbha’s chariot be yoked with lions whose manes are stained with divine blood, who seize upon snakes writhing in their locks, and whose faces are shrouded in darkness created by illusion.
He stirs up indignation, sets aside even the heavy good deeds of his master, and shakes off the pride of others; his hand is placed upon the hilt of his sword,
all his powers are prepared, the clamor cannot be endured, and his heart grows weary.
While the celestial women, having descended from the archways of their palaces, were offering ornaments,
and while the delighted host of night-stalkers was joyfully preparing for battle,
the monkey army approached and surrounded Rāghava on all sides.
The monkeys leap over the city of the night-stalkers, which has lost its splendor as its gardens and palaces have been shattered and its inhabitants have fled; it is stripped of its beauty,
like a woman whose garments have fallen away, while the steadfast lord of the monkeys holds it fast.
The wives of the gods behold the city of the night-stalkers, which is being savored by the monkey host—its uneven path trampled by the army of monkeys who have emerged in a rage;
where the gods cling to the sky out of fear for the whims of the proud monkey hosts as they rush about; and which must be seen with a sense of veneration.

As the monkeys set out for the battle, the trees— first shattered by the mountain peaks split open by their great speed and then falling along the path expected by those who waited— crash down upon the forest-dwellers,
who are obscured by the masses of dust raised from the surface of the sky.
The cries of lamentation arise, sounding like the rattling of the temples of elephants bound with fetters;
following the wind, the dust of the earth, heavy as it is cast up from the ground, swirls along,
resembling the uneven crash of trees broken by the force of the army as they stumble and turn back.
Those footprints of Mahendra,

planted long ago upon the mountain ridges, now provide for the nearby caves— overwhelmed by the crumbling slopes and the cascading torrents flowing toward the quarters of the sky— a state of being like a protective barrier.

But that city of the night-stalkers was shattered by monkeys restless in tearing down the gate-towers; with only the fire-stacks remaining within the walls and the palaces extinguished as the monkey-host momentarily overturned the ramparts, the splendor of the Lord of Rākṣasas was quenched.

Surrounded by monkeys standing so close together as to resemble a dense mountain thicket, the city of the Rākṣasas became like a fortress with its gates broken down and its ramparts collapsed in the midst of the invasion; then that monkey army, with its vast forces turning back and its gates shattered, [advanced].
The monkey hosts began to leap across the shore, which was formed by a continuous circle of Lanka’s ramparts;

they were like a second Suvela mountain attempting to cross a second ocean, as deep as the abyss of the underworld, within the whirlpool of the city's fortifications where a second mountain had been bound.
But immediately, when the abode of the Ten-faced one was overrun by the monkeys,
the nocturnal host broke loose with a great clamor and set forth like the waters of the ocean surging over the earth when shaken by the fire at the end of an aeon;
he [Rāvaṇa] mounts his chariot and departs, as it sways under the leaping of the elephants nearby.
With his temples smeared with flowing rut, his mane disheveled by the friction of the yoke,
somehow having fastened his armor, accompanied by a host of monkeys gathered for the fray,
and urging on his horses with the twang of his bowstring, Pādaṅghri goes forth in his chariot.
A multitude of swift horses, with yokes as broad as the walls of golden houses, has spread out like a single region of the city of Rākṣasa;
the chariot has horses that for a moment become lions, for a moment appear as elephants, and in another moment are buffaloes.
In that very moment, his chariots and horses, swift as mountains, carry him away;
yet when he has departed without being dismissed,
even the violation of Rāvaṇa’s command brings immediate joy to his own army, which is resonant with the tumultuous agitation of the assembly hall.
The army of the night-stalkers shone, with its warriors already arrayed and being further arrayed;
its chariots already yoked and engaged in combat; its elephant-hosts already formed and being further formed; its cavalry already set in motion and galloping forth;
with Rāma led by his elephant and Soma by his chariot, and the lord of the monkeys accompanied by his chariot and elephant.
The army, with Hanumān distinguished by his aerial flight and the host of monkeys distinguished by their movement on the ground, departs;

the force, jostled by the collision of chariots, with its elephant divisions being crowded together at the gate-mouths, surging through the intervals between the houses, turns back as it cannot find a single exit.

With difficulty, the chariots of the Rākṣasas— whose side-doors were forced open by the pressure of the turning yokes and poles— rush forward, their flagstaffs bent at an angle with the tops of their turrets tilted; they crush the elephants of the quarters, shatter the hoods of serpents, and trample the very foundations of the underworld.
The earth bears even the heavy burden of the Rākṣasas, which has become light due to its haste;

the army marches forth with its vanguard fallen upon the ground, its center crowded and blocked by the gates, its front filled with the breath of the Sāhis, and its courtyards overflowing with houses.
As he leads the vast army of night-stalkers toward the gateway pillar,
that host— spreading out like rivers flowing from a single mountain cleft onto level ground—
attains in an instant the beauty of the sandy banks of a river at the end of the rainy season, when its waters have been exhausted.
Having seen the courtyards of the Rākṣasa dwellings empty of warriors who were facing the battle, and observing the Rākṣasa folk emerging through the gates in haste due to the siege of Laṅkā,
the host of monkeys rushed forward like a forest fire driven by a fierce wind.
The night-stalker army increases its combat readiness, with its cavalry spreading out in all directions, its elephants freed from their goads, and the reins of its chariots loosened; thus,
in a single surge, they advance one after another, planting their feet firmly upon the earth.
The army of monkeys, having set out in a circular formation with its warriors undaunted, advances; and those warriors, possessing costly martial valor,
being urged on by their fury, both slay and are slain, yet they do not break solely because of their devotion.
In this great poem, *The Slaying of the Ten-Faced One*, composed by Śrī Pravarasena, the twelfth and thirteenth cantos [conclude].
Now,
with those who had gone out having returned and those who were already present having gathered together, they raised a great shout.
The heavy expedition for battle, granted and endured by the night-stalkers and the monkeys,
was thus slightly delayed as they moved one after another, eager for the fray, yet hastening with their feet placed upon the bodies of those slain before them.
Just as it was resolved in hearts turbid with rage, and just as it was manifested by eyes reddened with anger,
so too was the weapon hurled at the opponent on the battlefield; with speed exceeding that of their feet, they brandished their unsheathed swords in their fists.
The elephants, having acquired their mark through truth and being experts at the first blow, do not break even when struck;
they shake off the trees with their moving trunks, tossing the dust from their faces as they rub against the frontal globes,
and they uproot the trees with the force of their hands like those of a monkey.
Simultaneously, the equally fitting and terrible conclusion has come for both: for Rāma, the descendant of Daśaratha; for Māraṇa, the unbearable lord of the Rākṣasas;
and for the chariot-warriors, they are being slain by foot-soldiers with their feet, by horses with their horses, and by chariots with their chariots.
The monkeys have become the adversaries and the demon army their weapons;
with great mountains scattered by arrows and the remaining mountain-clutching mallets shattered by shafts,
the night-stalkers wander about, their arms crushed like crumbled peaks along the paths of those weapons.
Though fallen upon the broad shoulders of the monkey, which are as vast as the expanse of the Vindhya mountains,

the mass of the elephant’s thick trunk leaps up, unable to encircle them, as it is crushed by the chest of the Rākṣasa and hurled away by the fury of the monkeys who have pulverized the mountain peaks.
Dust rises upward, while a mass of stones falls downward;

in the midst of the enemy host, heroes are seen being struck down without interval as they advance with undaunted valor; the paths of the elephants, difficult even for warriors to behold, are marked by their extraordinary prowess.
He breathes with courage; light-handed and unimpeded, he strikes and laughs; his enmity increases; he performs great feats of violence;
he does not falter even when his head falls; and though pierced by agony, his heart does not break.
The fear of battle does not cling to those of perverse intellect even when it is being instilled;
pride endures amidst blows; the assembly of men endures at places of arrogance; and the essence of wrath does not recede even during the blameless retreats of warriors.
With their manes tossed upward as they leap from the riverbank, their thick tufts of mane quivering with rage,
and their teeth firmly gnashing at the roots, the lions roar with envy and close their eyes; yet,
one must not show contempt for them, for even in the face of danger, one remembers the master’s noble deeds.
Death is not reckoned with, nor is fear remembered even when danger is seen; those very same netherworld-dwellers who were long ago cast aside by the first wives even at the risk of their own lives,
have now been pursued by celestial nymphs as they fell face-to-face in battle.
With his gaze fixed on the enemy host, his limbs pale from the flow of unceasing blood, and disregarding the agony of his wounds, he savors the taste of hot blows; who does not tremble?
For they do not wait for an opportunity, but strike down the enemy as soon as their transgression is committed.
As they promised, they entered before the shouts of acclaim, capable of [preserving] their noble lineage; thus,
that [palace] manifested itself to them as the appointed chamber for attaining union with the celestial nymphs.
The battle, which shattered the necklaces of the world, whose course was directed toward the palace of Mahendra,
where the tusks of elephants— crushed against the chests of monkey-warriors and their own faces— were splintered,
and where the mountain paths were resonant with the moving bracelets of celestial wives falling upon the dust of slain warriors.
A battle where the elephants were scattered by the discharge of arrows,
where horses were seized and then abandoned, where the demon warriors were slain by pursuing monkeys,
and where the blows from sandalwood trees were endured with relief as they quenched the heat of the battlefield.

The sound of arrows passing through mouths opened wide with a gurgling roar, the breaking and mending of pots, foot soldiers retreating and then rallying back, chariot-processions drenched in blood, and horses silent with foam from their parched mouths; kalaala-lohugghāḍia-muha-bolīṇa-sara-magga-ṇinta-ṇiṇāaṃ bhiṇṇa-ghaḍijjanta-ghaḍaṃ paḍiruddhosaria-cakkalia-pāikkaṃ ruhirohiṇṇa-raha-vahaṃ muha-sukkha-ppheṇa-ṇihua-hesia-turaaṃ

The sound of "well done! resounded, pregnant with the joy of those struck by the mountain; the shouts of warriors fell silent as they fainted from the wounds of the shattered mountain, while the cries of the soldiers seeking the elephants were stifled by the agony of being uprooted by the blows of the rock.
The chariot is being recognized with difficulty by its own soldiers, who have lost their way, become bewildered by the shattered standards, and are suffering;
the horses are neighing as they stumble, their faces cast down and exhausted from pulling the chariot pushed against the mountain;
and the pale blood is broken and smeared with the red juice of the mountain crushed upon the surface of the earth.
The path of the fresh river was discernible through the heaps of crushed stones cast aside;

the road was strewn with the discarded armor and weapons of those who had fled; monkeys and warriors were falling upon one another as they rushed forward; and there arose a tumultuous cloud of golden manes tossed about by the leaping monkeys.
The battlefield, where the earth was pierced by the bodies of warriors split by weapons fallen at midday;
where monkeys, seizing the heads of night-stalkers and biting their chests, had set down their fangs;
and where the dust was heavy with the weight of being drenched by the cool spray from mountain torrents held aloft by the claws.
Chariots, overturned by horses that bolted when struck by the driver’s whip,

are being dragged away; meanwhile, unbearable cries of distress arise from those who, being shattered, are half-dragged back while their blood flows in streams like mountain torrents broken by the impact of arrows.
With their mouths silenced and their opposing ranks shattered, the night-stalkers—
whose weapons of sword and missile were broken by the monkeys' blows and whose targets could no longer be distinguished—
though being dragged away, continue to cling to one another with eyes closed in a swoon.
Crushed by the heavy assault, the monkey-warrior shines forth— rendered helpless by the Rākṣasa who has not yet been subdued; his armor shattered, fallen after being torn from the ranks,
his majesty destroyed by the heroism of the foe, his shadow [vanished] by the blows of valor, and his followers scattered.
By life, pride is preserved; by the body, great fame is maintained;
the chest is broken by a mountain, but not the heart; the chariot is destroyed, but not the warrior's enthusiasm; the lofty head-wounds are inflicted, but not the battle-longings of the heroes.

In the sky, the spreading red dust of the earth is being washed away by mountain torrents; on the paths of the rain, it is being washed away by the streams of rut-fluid from elephants; and in the water-jars, it is being washed away by the overflowing liquid.
Having endured the blows of swords, the frontal globes of the lordly elephants appear like scars carved by their own tusks.
Bent by the friction of the whetstone, the arrow-shaft breaks unevenly; though parched for a long time,
the bird does not drink the harsh, molten iron that overflows from the mouth of the furnace while it is being tempered for the sword-blade, even after pecking at it.
Even when fallen and pierced by arrows, he maintains his indignation as long as his speech remains clear;
even a headless trunk with its severed head still runs on; it offers a taste of blood from its upraised throat; the enemy's blow carries the burden of his valor; the mass of enmity persists.
Increasing his fury in battle upon being attacked, he augments his pride;

he bears an excessive burden like an enemy, does not tolerate an insult as if it were dishonor, suffers no delay as if it were happiness, gives up his life as if it were a mere loss, and strikes directly at his opponent like a warrior with a weapon.

The monkeys, having endured sword-strokes, their arms shattered and drained of blood, fainting and collapsing upon their own mountain peaks, offer up their pride like a flower; yet they cannot believe that their glory is increasing and remains unblemished.
The host of warriors, disregarding the weight of the world, makes an effort for life alone;
once their own path of the sword-edge has been clearly perceived,
they are able to enter the heavy enemy throng, which increases in mass as it grows, with speed.
They bear the burden of their fame; they do not tolerate the humiliation of their prowess; they exercise restraint over their anger; they increase their pride; they are capable of daring deeds;
and they possess a joy born of the first blow, though it is a happiness whose desire for battle has melted away in an instant of fainting.
In battle, one displays the blood acquired with life and fame turned about upon the head;

in doubts, one laughs; in daring deeds, one rejoices; in calamities, one delights; in fainting fits, one rests; and only when it is said "it has been accomplished," is one counted as having succeeded—even unto death.
And it moved on, struck by the feet [of the sun], with its apprehension of seizing the moon’s orb dispelled;
having dragged the night to its setting, it shattered the day with its absence;
it was thick with dust at its base, while in its middle region it possessed lightning-like streaks due to its spreading nature.
Spread across the mass of clouds, the dust of the earth falls into the quarters; by its weight, it seems to release the earth and fill it, yet it goes out from the quarters and seems to support them.
With its path of departure unseen, the dust falls from the sky, yet it clings to the heavens.
The army of the night-stalkers (demons) is seen, its radiance eclipsed by the thick ranks of the monkey warriors;
standing before the mountain of jewels (Rāvaṇa), it appears like the luster of a fallen meteor.
With the dust of trampled elephants rising up and the foam from the mouths of crushed horses spreading abroad, it advances.
Like a dark cloud, thin in the sky and possessing a dusky luster, the mass of rays of the sun—
its path through the firmament blocked by the mountains hurled down by the impetuosity of the monkeys—
falls with a turbid brilliance like a stream from a mountain spring.

In the streams of blood flowing from the broad shoulders of the mountain-dwelling demons, who were torn apart by the arrows of Kṛtānta, the sun— exhausted and weary from wandering through the battlefield, its rays dimmed and its eyes closed— is now clinging with passion, like a bee in a thick honeycomb.
The lords of elephants, their faces smeared with dust mingled with frost,
their trunks formidable as they uproot [trees], and with streams of blood spreading through the intervals between them,
fall together one by one upon the earth, crushing it beneath their weight.
Having dried the clouds in the sky, the wind draws out the uneven streaks of dust— grey from the tracks of herds of cows moving along the paths of shade—
and thins the columns of smoke rising from the burning forests; meanwhile,
at the front of the battle, it obstructs the line of sight of the elephants charging toward one another.
Shaken by the wind of Mārua, Mahiratha was first struck down like a mouth-cloth at the edge of the speech;
then, by the river of blood gushing forth from the path of the forest of the warriors' chest-wounds,
Mahiratha was swept away like a tree uprooted from its bank.
The moonlight, resembling the frost of a Palāśa flower, flickers as it is slightly interrupted—
scattered by the wind, remaining in a thin layer,
like the remnants of dust following a straight path, resembling the flow of a river turning between mountains.
The monkeys fall,

having performed difficult tasks and sent on perilous errands; they have crushed impassable paths, borne the burden of battle while clinging tenaciously and enduring unbearable blows, and they pass through the midst of fallen herds of elephants as they scale the mountain whose peaks are crumbling.

The battle increases— a bond of enmity tied by kinsmen, a source of joy for the headless trunks that complete their thousands, providing sustenance for the warriors, marked by the falling of heroes with arms as powerful as tree-trunks,
and encircled by the rings of armor gathered at the wrists and severed from the body.
The yak-tail ornaments, heavy with their roots severed, cannot be led by the night-stalker; falling down, they hang from his blood-dripping jaws, bound by cords,
their eyelashes dripping and weighted down by the foam.
With their trunks raised upward and released, the hindquarters sagging under the weight of the front half,
the lords of the herd shake their upraised goads— which were sinking into the frontal globes marked by the stone-like scars of the thunderbolt— while the elephants,
overwhelmed by the burden of the monkeys, are intent on delivering blows to break the onslaught of the gods.
The night-stalker army has become visible; facing the enemy, their first onset was difficult to withstand.

Their elephants have turned back with their trunks curled, their chariots have spun around and been shattered by the shifting of positions, their warriors have retreated on a single step, and their horses have been brought to a gallop in circular maneuvers.
The night-stalkers, having been dragged away by their fury, fled after wandering about and losing their anger;
with their monkeys slightly startled and cast off, they retreated into the caves, while the chariots were yoked to horses and the foot-soldiers stumbled over the backs of the peacock-like steeds.
The monkey army turns back, crowded with chariots being overturned by elephants,
trumpeting with uneven and violent agitation; their arms hang down heavily as they break off trees, their rival warriors flee in distress, and the night-stalkers are driven away.
With their heroism unbroken and having brought about the first occasion for the shattering of pride, the Rākṣasas, though defeated, wander about once more; they do not feel even the slightest fear.

Nevertheless, he whose heavy chariot with its wheels was being turned by only slightly revolving circles, who had acquired the glory of battle through the exertion of restraining those who had fled in all directions,
and who had the faces of the night-stalkers (Rākṣasas) bent and half-broken as they turned away from the monkeys— [he, Rāvaṇa].
The army, with its masses of elephants retreating at the sound of the enemy's roar;
with horses standing motionless while being held by their tails by fleeing monkeys who were running after them;
and with chariots being dragged away by horses terrified by monkeys who had killed the warriors and fallen upon the charioteers.
The army of night-stalkers was shattered; its path was obscured by the sparse cries of those whose strength was spent as they fell upon the road of the torrential downpour.
With their weapons slipping from their hands, their arms became empty, and their hearts were lightened by envy while their eyes were fixed solely on protecting one another.

The night-stalkers, with their ten heads fallen at heart, have turned back, abandoned the fear of battle, and their fame for alliance is severed; having set aside their courage as they retreated from the front,
they are difficult for the monkey host to overcome, their commitment to the burden of war slackened.
A battle involving elite warriors rages between the monkeys and the night-stalkers; the former are ashamed of defeat while the latter are delighted by their increasing momentum.
Sugrīva, who finds joy in battle, has granted the privilege of combat to Pādaṅghri, who stands beneath the Saptacchada tree.

In battle, struck by the fragrant ichor of the forest-elephant— which was like a loud burst of laughter from blossoming jasmine— the life of Asaniprabha, who lay fallen upon his chest smeared with the scent of fresh sandalwood, departed as he breathed in that fragrance and closed his eyes in blissful sleep.
Having struck Vajramuṣṭi with his fist, the lord of monkeys laughed as the other’s eyes burst open,
copper-red with flames issuing from his wrathful gaze, shattered by the blow of that fist;
thus was Vajramuṣṭi, who had long fought and rejoiced, defeated by Suseṇa.
With his two feet raised up by Nala,

who had seized them with his nails, the sun’s body was struck; though he endured the blow, his head was pressed against the surface of the sun’s body with such force that his neck was broken, and his body was cast half-way down onto the ground.
Having swiftly slain Jambumālin, the son of the Wind (Hanuman) shattered Añjika;
with the ten directions drenched by the blood gushing from his head, which was split by the crushing blow of the entire palm tree,
he then reached the height of his martial prowess in the battle against the sons of Indrajit and Vāli.
The monkey excels the other [Rāvaṇa], who has his own attendants holding the scales for weighing him one by one,
who has blinded the quarters with arrows, and who is surrounded by a circle of bows, by means of thousands of mountains brought forth from the lookout-towers, released, and falling down.
The clusters of trees— laden with bees clinging to their bending branches heavy with flowers, lightened by the scattered fruit, and with shoots shaken from their midsections—
fall toward the daughter of the Wind; yet the mass of arrows does not reach her in the sky, for it is dispersed by the trees.

As they proceed along the forest path, the trees—showering scattered lodhra blossoms, wafting the fragrance of sandalwood crushed by the arrows, scattering mandāra flowers, and heavy with fresh cloves—are being torn asunder; yet they do not overstep the son of the Ten-faced One.
Thus does the sky become.
Thus,
that battle— where hands were struck evenly together and shouts of "Bravo! were given repeatedly by both sides—
increased even though it had reached its ultimate limit for the sons of Indrajit and Vālin.
The son of Vālin, having flown up into the vault of the sky filled with arrows discharged by the son of the Ten-faced One,
was watched with astonishment by an army whose ranks were startled as they stood still, their activities suspended,
while bees were driven away by the shafts emerging from the midst of the *dūma* flowers and clinging to his feathered arrows.
The son of Daśamukha was blocked by the mountain of stone and *sāla* trees crushed by Vālin’s son in his rage;

the quarters of the sky were reddened by the blood of the monkeys’ bodies torn open by the arrows of the night-stalkers; and the surface of the earth was made muddy with the blood of the rākṣasas wounded by the blows of the monkeys.
The army of the night-stalkers was distressed by the river-pain [of their own wounds], given cause for grief among the monkeys by the abduction of Vālin’s son,
its ranks shattered by the fear of the son of Daśamukha who had fainted from the blow of the mountain,
and it resounded with the clamor of the monkey host as they exerted themselves against the night-stalkers led by the son of Tārā.

The world of the Rākṣasas was filled with the faces of demons whose joy at the death of their son Mandodarī had vanished; it mocked the monkey warriors with the effortless shattering of mountain peaks that fell like fruitless stones; and the sky was whitened by the loud laughter emitted from the mouths of the mountain crags split open upon their chests.

Now, when Indrajit, the son of Vālin, was slain—his enthusiasm broken by his passion for battle—the poets laugh, saying he was killed through trickery; the Rākṣasas rejoice, thinking he remained alive.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter.
The fourteenth day of consolation has dawned;
now that the days have passed fruitlessly, Rāghava, facing Laṅkā with his exhausted Rākṣasas sinking in despair, grieves as he awaits the arrival of the Ten-faced one according to his desire.

Thinking, "Dasāṇaṇa does not go to battle while seated comfortably upon these," he desires to fix his gaze upon the jewel-studded quivers with their arrows provided; and as the enemy approaches, he watches the volleys of arrows being discharged.
In the battle, the monkeys wander about, exhausted and their trees shattered; having broken through the masses of rocks hurled swiftly and driven back,
Rāma’s arrows first fulfill their purpose and then shatter the hopes of the opposing monkeys.
The weapon of the rākṣasa was shattered along with his own arm, and though hurled swiftly, it did not reach the monkey; for the monkey’s weapon—
a stone— struck the chest of the rākṣasa, and the mountain peak, having been severed and cast down, struck off his head.
The earth is strewn with arrows released in anger by monkeys whose prowess was joined with haste;
yet the arrow of the Lord of the Raghus remains fixed as if joined once more, and his bow remains drawn into a circle,
while the ground is covered by the heads of Rākṣasas falling repeatedly upon the arrows.

The paths of his arrows are seen upon the bodies of the Rākṣasas like unevenly kindled fires, like the openings of holes inhabited by venomous serpents; yet no arrows are seen in the hand of him as he draws them back,
in the heart of him as he aims, or in the mouth of him as he roars.
Only the fallen arrows of Rāma are seen, indicated by the wounds upon their heads;
wherever he was seen, wherever his cry was heard, wherever he was broken,
and wherever he moved, there indeed have the arrows of Rāma fallen.
In that Rākṣasa army, elephants, warriors, and horses appear long as they stand at the front ranks; having broken the bank, the arrows of Rāma have emerged,
and whatever fear they shall produce, it must be faced with the simultaneous commencement of battle.
Seeing that army of night-stalkers struck down by Rāma’s arrows and fallen, the Lord of the Raghus,
in an instant, reduced the host of Rākṣasas to nothing but their names and Sāraṇa— having seen the mass of their heads falling at the very same moment the arrows pierced them.
Meanwhile, the twilight darkness— indistinguishable from the army of the blood-red Rākṣasas—
was effectively extinguished after a long time; and now the day has dawned, its fear of the Rākṣasa vanished,
having raised its banner alone, with the son of Vālin having crushed the chariot of Rāvaṇa’s son.
As he moves through the sky, which has its darkness melted away by his own radiance,
the night-stalkers— whose roots of heavy enmity have been destroyed by Indra—
are simultaneously perceived like tender sprouts by Fate, though it remains unseen.
And he drank those arrows given by Śambhu— arrows whose tongues were the fire issuing from the mouths of serpents—
which had pierced the bodies of Aṅgada,
as he lay with his arms hanging down in confidence after slaying all the Rākṣasas, his face revealed as his second arm was torn away.
Stationed upon Rāghava’s body, their arms fixed by the three [points], these lordly serpents— serving as arrows,
dark blue with dripping venom, their mouths ablaze with sparks from the fire of poison—
are discharged from the bow; possessing the grace of unprecedented iron shafts, they fly forth.
Flashes of lightning, bright as the gleam of iron rods exceeding the stars,
fall like arrows from dark clouds that veil the sky like demon-hosts;
first resembling the solar disc and then like meteors, they descend across the mid-heavens.
The lakes are being split apart, their beds revealed; serpents are caught upon the branches;
young deer, their hopes shattered by fear, perish;
the rutting elephants wander about with their secretions unseen; and the monkeys roam with their mountain peaks uplifted.

The night-stalker licks the sky; the monkey host in the quarters is pierced through and through in their hearts; yet the son of Daśaratha, his eyes fixed upon the sight of the enemy, does not break even while being shattered—[he who is] ablaze with the fire of wrath, a replica of the flaming submarine fire.
The serpents, having gained full range over his limbs, merely encircle his heart;

their coils, formed by the embrace of those snakes, have become firm and motionless like sandalwood trees growing on the slopes of Mount Malaya, entwined by the coils of serpents whose massive bodies swell with agony.
Thus, having taken up their bows and arrows, with the surfaces of their motionless arms pierced by shafts, their futile rage indicated merely by their bitten lips,
the sons of Raghu—
light-footed— made themselves visible as their bodies were pierced by arrows, becoming objects to be sought out by the gaze.
The two broad thighs of Rāma’s son, stained with blood from the arrow-head lodged deep within them,
his feet remaining motionless and paralyzed by the piercing pain,
and his body’s strength utterly exhausted— Rāma’s son must move even while thus struck down.

And suddenly, his bow was raised by those with hearts like that of gods, who— having been struck by arrows discharged by an invisible enemy— had their left hands restrained by the impact of those shafts; thus, while the first arrows remained fixed and faltering, he leaped up toward the rear part of the terrace of the trembling celestial chariot.

Then Rāhu fell, his throat pierced by the sharp fangs of the gods, his lute-stringing groaning as he was crushed by a single mouth, shattering the bond of hope for the three worlds like a forest elephant struck by a lion’s tusk-goad at a tall nearby tree.
And as the Lord of the Rākṣasas fell, the son of Sumitrā followed him along his path;

he was like the mass of shade falling from a tree that has been uprooted and cast down, while those two, having fallen upon the earth, turned their faces toward one another with their weight sinking down in exhaustion.
With one wheel turned upward, its triangular surface facing the gods, the chariot remained for a long time as if paralyzed by the fall of Rāma’s heart; suddenly, as if struck by the fall of night,
the triple world fell into darkness as if life had departed from its head.

Alas! The monkey army—despondent, its vigor shattered, its heart pierced by despair, and its mind agitated—does not abandon Rāghava even though he has fallen; it remains motionless with fear, piling itself up, devoid of hope as it gazes toward the empty quarters of the sky, awaiting protection from Rāma.
With his eyes fixed upon Rāghava as if he were a painted figure, the monkey host remains motionless; yet,
even as he falls, the radiance of the face of the Lord of the Raghus, appearing before him—
enhanced by his lack of despondency and sustained by constant fortitude— seems to converse with the Lord of the Monkeys.
But then, by the Lord of Monkeys, whose eyes were like the waters of the ocean of Vihīṣaṇa,
the son of Daśānana was seen nearby in the sky with his bow ready; having been dispatched, Suggīva rushed forward, leaping as if he were tearing apart thousands of mountains with his fury.
Having merely overrun Laṅkā, which was trembling with fear, the lord of the night-stalkers (Rāvaṇa) remained there;
delighted by the report from Indrajit regarding the death of Rāghava,
and comforted by having discovered a means for the reunion with Janaka’s daughter, he sighed a sigh of relief.
Then, having been brought before the ten-faced Rāvaṇa by the night-stalkers, the daughter of Janaka— having witnessed her own fresh moment of misfortune,
crying out with a broken voice, fainting from her distress, and now emerging from her swoon—
was seen by Rāghava as he beheld the son of Sumitrā.
He began to lament, his heart instantly shattered by the loss of Sītā;
even that Laksmaṇa, upon whom the entire three worlds rested with confidence when he ascended his bow, has been slain.
There is nothing in this forest that the transformation of fate does not reach.
"Or rather, my brother-in-law Sugrīva, who has accomplished his task for my sake and has cast away his life,
has only made himself light by bearing the burden of arms fruitlessly;
then he spoke sweetly to Sugrīva, revealing his resolve through his encouragement."
O steadfast one, you have uttered words that are profound, established even in the state of sudden death,
and resolute; and this host of monkeys, whose strength lies in their arms,
has also performed a deed difficult to achieve even for one whose fame is preeminent in the world, by means of Māruti.
Since the royal splendor of Vibhīṣaṇa has not been brought under my control— thereby binding the enmity of our kin—
and since this sorrow has made my heart feel the taste of unbearable arrow-pain, you must go; do not falter, for you must proceed swiftly by that very bridge.
Behold the circle of kinsmen; having understood the transformation brought about by the passage of time,
the lord of monkeys, his face distorted by intense rage and his arms constricted by the pain of weeping,
spoke this reply to the Lord of the Raghus without first giving [the gift] to the monkeys.
Speak of him who is endowed with auspicious marks, whose hero’s bed was fashioned from fresh sprouts;
reach the monkey host, and [convey] the final verses to the Lord of the Raghus, whose pain from the arrow has not yet subsided.

And I too—having seized my bow, which was drawn back with a speed surpassing the falling of lightning; having shattered the enemy's chariot by brandishing and bending my arm, which was half-turned and drawn back; and having my pair of hands, resting upon my shoulder, grasping the sword Candahāsa with its blade unsheathed—[rushed forward].

With chariots struck, crushed, and smashed by his trampling feet, their weapons falling away as they retreated; with the front ranks broken and their arms rendered useless and disarrayed, their remaining hands fruitless; and with their chests split open by powerful fists falling like thunderbolts upon their hands— The provided text describes a scene of chaotic battle and destruction. Here is the polished translation: Chariots were trampled, struck, and crushed beneath his advancing feet, causing their weapons to fall away as they fled;
the vanguard was shattered, their pairs of arms thrown into disarray and rendered useless; and their chests were split open by powerful fists falling like thunderbolts upon their hands.

"I shall make the Ten-faced one's head torn away, dragged out, crushed, and scattered one by one, his heart shattered by nails joined with fruitless arrows; thus, this very day, when Daśānana has been slain by me, I shall return to Kiṣkindhā."
Janaka’s daughter will either die a slow death or witness Rāghava dying;
thus, when these arrows of the poison-snake were warded off by Vibhīṣaṇa, Suggīva began to recite a Gāruḍa mantra within his heart, and Rāghava [did the same].
But now the surface of the earth has become a chariot, with Mount Suvela shaken by the ocean's edge as it is suddenly seized, and the corpses of Rākṣasas scattered by the harsh winds.
And he beholds [the peacock], which has dispelled the great darkness with the thick radiance of its golden plumage;
whose eyelashes are as soft as fresh feathers; upon whose firm back rests the path of the seat of the Great Lord (Indra);
and whose chest is revealed by a single feather loosened by the blow of Indra’s irresistible weapon.
Rāma [discharges arrows] at Garuḍa, whose breast-ornament is turning as his neck is being pierced;
then, when Garuḍa has performed his salutation to Rāma and stands facing him with his eyes fixed upon him,
the two of them stand with their bodies relaxed, and it cannot be discerned where the masses of arrows have gone.

Then the Lord of the Raghus, freed from the bond of arrows and devoid of the exhaustion caused by his employment of the *vinata* weapon, became one who possessed the power of his own self, as formidable as the elephant or the Garuda.
Hearing that the Lord of the Raghus was freed from the bond of arrows, the Lord of the Night-stalkers [acted].
Fearing Garuda, he casts his entire burden of battle upon Dhūmrākṣa;
with fury as if with a chariot, or with impetuosity as if with the army of the night-stalkers (Rākṣasas), he goes forth, bearing joy like an arm and hostility toward his enemies like valor.

Then that host of Rākṣasas, together with Dhumrakṣa, resembling the surging ocean, stood upon the path of the wind-god’s movement— as if before the submarine fire— while the fierce conclusion of the conflict between the monkey and Rākṣasa armies was being prepared.
Then Dhūmrākṣa, whose eyes were clouded with smoke, overwhelmed Māruti with arrows, his store of weapons inexhaustible;

but the monkey laughed, shaking off the impact of those shafts which proved fruitless as they merely caught in the hair between his brows, having crushed and bent Rāvaṇa’s chariot under his assault, and standing firm with Dhūmrākṣa’s bow against his chest.
The stone has shattered on the ground; the pestle, crushed by the leaping calf, is no longer desired;
and the weapon, released by the monkey with eyes red with rage, lies scattered here and there as a mere scrap of iron.
With his long left hand forming a coil around his neck as it bent down,
the lion’s roar resounded from within his chest as he struggled to keep his life-force from escaping;
for a moment, his hands were rendered useless and agitated, his weapons falling away as they slipped from his grasp.
The son of the Wind-god reduced Dhūmrākṣa— who had risen up and abandoned all hope for life— to the state of a mere gust of wind.
Then, when Dhūmrākṣa had fallen and the remainder of the night-stalker army had departed,
the son of the Wind beheld Akampana proceeding toward the presence of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa) at his command.

Hanumān also casts down that [host], whose multitude of weapons has been rendered useless by being fearlessly snatched away from their broad chests; its equipment is shattered and scattered one by one.
Then, dispatched by the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), he is struck and hurled forth, colliding with equal force against Hanumān’s blow.

Falling into the mouth of Nīla— who was distressed by not having obtained the joy of battle— the arrow, released by the desperate Prahasta, fell upon Nīla’s chest at the very moment of departure; it was signaled by the gushing flow of blood bursting through the wound.
A certain poet beholds the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṇa), its branches bent down, fragrant with the scent of the gods' elephants, with bees clinging to its path through the air,
and its shoots extended against the wind; it resembles a mass of raindrops from a thundercloud as it passes by.
