Then, as he stood upon the path of the [falling] tree, a shower of pearl-like fruits shaken from its branches was released by his arm; it fell like a broken cascade of pearls filling the forest, upon a chest drenched with blood from the blows of falling branches that shattered the white blossoms.

Simultaneously, arrows fell upon the trees; simultaneously, monkeys covered the surface of the sky with trees; and simultaneously, by him, a manifest mass of rocks was discharged in the four directions—[rocks] from which trees were breaking apart and masses of stone were shattering under the impact of the arrows.
The regions of the sky are seen where mountain torrents are severed by crumbling peaks;

the sky appears dark blue like a water-laden cloud, streaked with the twilight glow and thick with masses of golden filaments scattered across its slopes, turbid with the red hue of mountain minerals.
Just then, at the edge of the sky, the monkey appeared as if held steady by the masses of arrows first released from his bow, which was drawn back and then turned away; then,
with his sword, he struck Nīla’s forehead with a mace that rebounded from it.
In the midst [of the sea], the Son of Fire (Vaiśravaṇa) seizes a black rock that resounds as it is held, which has been brought here with haste and deception,
and which possesses a hardness and breadth equal to the vast and expansive chest of a powerful man, appearing like a cloud clinging to the peak of Mount Suvela.

When the sun had set upon the mountain slope and had risen far away in the blue sky, day was born in the heavens and night, with its darkness instantly formed, appeared upon the surface of the earth; then,
out of his passion for battle, Nīla endured a heavy blow from the enemy.
Split within by his own wounds, with life-blood trickling away, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, and begins the fifteenth canto, in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha* composed by the illustrious Pravarasena.
Then, when Prahasta was slain, Rāvaṇa— his arms constricted by the fury arising from the slaughter of his kinsman—
advanced, filling the ten directions with his lion-like roars and *huṃkāras*;
likewise, the enraged one laughed, filling the ten directions with the caverns of his terrifying mouths.
Just as his attendants had become silent with fear and hidden among the pillars of the palace, he mounted the chariot, whose rear panel was bent by the weight of his feet,
which was being held back by the charioteer, and which possessed a troop of restless horses.
By the sound of the *huṃ* uttered with a great clamor that shook Sahā, and by the clamor of the city's army within Laṅkā, it was known by the monkeys that the Ten-faced One had set out;
only then did he appear, his shadow darkened by the white parasols held over the multitude of his faces due to the intensity of his suffering.

Having emerged from the city, the monkey host— its pride in battle shattered— is broken; then, with their shoulders pressed against the tips of the tufts of their tails as they turn back by the mere force of their mouths, the throngs of monkeys, clinging to the path of the routed [enemy], behold Daśānana.

To those whose armor was shattered, whose feet were pierced by the arrows discharged by the Ten-faced One, and who had forgotten their original commands, the Son of Fire spoke as the fear of battle arose:
"Do not abandon the burden of the fray; here is the one who has raised up half of Mount Malaya!"
O charioteer, for whose sake you have set out, he himself is now snatching away your life!
And yet, though he was pointed out by the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) as "he," with his heart pierced by the arrows of Sītā,
Rāma was not looked upon for so long with such deep reverence as he was as "her beloved."
Then the Lord of the Night-dwellers, struck by Rāma’s arrows, his chariot being set on fire by the monkeys turning their backs, and his protective armor shattered, fled toward Laṅkā;
thus he attained diminished glory and abandoned his footing of valor through the destruction of his followers.
The awakening of Kumbhāṇḍa, who had fallen asleep comfortably during the night, was brought about by Ālaka;
and he too, yawning with his head heavy from the fatigue of waking at dawn, laughed for a long time and, hearing the light message regarding the slaying of Rāma...
The golden rampart of his body became crushed like the yoke of Rati’s chariot;
the golden girdle clinging to the region of his thighs seemed as if it were slightly loosened;
and for him who had leaped over the rampart, the sea-monsters were seized in their jaws, crying out in distress.
The ocean shores became knee-deep; seeing this,
the hosts of monkeys turned back even as they were looking on, abandoning their efforts in battle,
their mountain-bearers slipping from their hands and falling down.

Having struck the entire monkey army most violently with rocks, trees, stones, maces, and with staffs, weapons, missiles, and clubs, the Rakshasas, intoxicated by blood, in an instant [destroyed] the monkeys, the elephants, and the horses.
Shaken by the discharge of Rāma’s arrows, his own army began to flee from the enemy force.
As he had fought for a long time, both of his arms— struck first by the arrows shot from Rāma’s bow and then by streams of blood gushing from the wounds— collapsed to the ground.
One arm, like Mount Suvela, blocked the mouth of the river [of battle] and fell repeatedly,
having regained its strength from the ocean; the second remained like a second bridge for him,
drawn back by the enemy and with its crest of peacock feathers whirled at the front of the fray.
With its wheel as high as Rāhu’s head severed by the discus of the Lord of Rāhu,
and with its mouth-caverns resonant as it filled them with wind while raised toward the sky,
Trikuṭa appeared— as though its fourth lofty peak had emerged— even though it was broken and fallen.
When Kumbhakarṇa had fallen, the ocean— its grasp of the shore broken by fleeing in terror,
its shallow bed now filling its entire expanse— seemed to vomit forth the submarine fire;
and hearing of the destruction of Kumbhakarṇa, Daśānana was filled with excessive agitation.
Laughing again at him who was reddening with rage, she shook her mass of hair; and at that moment, as he advanced with his indignation increasing,
even those same locks, spreading across the space between the pillars on the terrace of the palace, were no longer sufficient for the expanse of his chest.
But immediately after he had departed from the house, his son Meghanāda— having opened the chest, filled the lap of the palace, and fallen upon his knees— stood up and laughed,
saying to him: "Even when a task requiring great daring has been accomplished by oneself, one must still be urged on by one's father."
A father does not find the touch of a son, nor the likeness of a son, even with his own son;
why then, while I yet live, do you destroy the fame of our very own Rakshasa clan for the sake of a mere human child, a tender youth?
Having uprooted the serpent-king (the ocean), having destroyed the Nandana grove, and having overturned the mountains,

you do not even recognize yourself— how much less the Lord of the Raghus, who alone with his arrows dried up the ocean and is capable of bearing the burden of the three worlds? Why do you wish to slay him in the face of battle?
"Today itself, I shall cast all seven into the ocean, whose submarine fire is surging;
thus informed by the Ten-faced One, the western charioteer placed his head in [Rāvaṇa's] hand."

Eager for battle, he mounts his chariot— the broad surface of its side-panels bent low by the weight of the advance of his feet, slow from the armor fastened upon them; wherefrom the sunbeams are scattered by the lightning discharged by clouds resting upon its high peaks— and hears the roar of Rāma’s bow close at hand.

With his face turned away, having cast off the burden [of the city] at the command of the Ten-faced One, the son of the Ten-faced One goes forth mounted on a chariot and surrounded by a retinue of Rākṣasas;
he who, at the gateway of the city of the Ten-faced One, was at the entrance of the city where the chariot had swiftly sped.
As he was testing the strength of his arms, that very same Vidyutjihva raised a great clamor; then,
with his attention fixed on Rāma, the son of Daśānana, his strength depleted by the foremost monkeys who had leaped up first, was hemmed in by the monkey warriors along with the son of Jvalana.
With his blue [arrow] he shatters the Gaṇḍa mountain, with his divine one the tree, and with his stone-tipped one the slab;
and with the Nala-arrow released together with his shafts, he breaks the peak-fragment of Mount Malaya.
Thus, the army of monkeys, its ranks shattered, sets out toward Niṣadha.
Vibhīṣaṇa said to the son of Sumitrā, "Restrain Meghanāda. Then, as he fought with illusory arrows and rocks,
the son of Sumitrā struck off the head of Meghanāda, who was like a Rākṣasa, with the hand of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Hearing of Indrajit’s slaughter, Daśānana wept tears of rage;
rising up, he fell instantly like a drop of ghee into a heated frying pan, as soon as Meghanāda was slain and he turned back, by Fate.
Struck by both hands as if by two simultaneous showers of arrows, the Ten-faced One—
whose kinsmen were all utterly slain— emerged like a host of Rākṣasas, terrifying with their multitude of faces and difficult to behold due to his many arms, though he was but a single being.
Furthermore, the battlefield has the sun obscured by the dense darkness of black clouds driven by the wind,
and the mass of manes of horses drenched by the rut-fluid from the temples of aged elephants.

Having mounted the chariot— the rear portion of which was adorned with the moon’s orb like a cluster of flowers on the great tree of Mount Meru, and which was streaked by the mass of flames rising from the friction of the chariot-pole—
and seeing it proceeding, the night-folk, their minds filled with auspicious joy, gazed upon it.
From the very moment they were born, those eyes have been a source of tears;

therefore, with his gaze and his arrows, he has equated the army of monkeys— which has quickly crossed the mountain slopes by means of water poured from the hollows of his palms— with the mountain torrents.
Even toward Vihīṣaṇa at Pāsāvaḍia, who was surrounded by a host of monkeys,
his arrow— though composed of the essence of indignation because [the enemy] was wretched and a kinsman—
leaps forth; yet, having endured the first blow, it is only now that, out of rage, it is joined with a prominent shaft.
Like a tree struck by Indra’s thunderbolt, Lakṣmaṇa was pierced in the chest by the spear;
yet, having received life from the mountain herbs brought by the son of the Wind-god,
he joined his arrow to his bow as before and began to fight with the night-stalkers.
And Rāma too gazes upon the mountain range, its cloud-like slopes shattered by the impact of the horses' hooves,
from which the fragrance of gold columns— resembling the wielder of the thunderbolt as he stands there— emanates.
The long shaft of the pole was bent down by the weight of the *mālatī* garland held in his left hand;
the tufts of the fly-whisks were lowered as they settled, wetted by the spray from the breaking droplets of clouds;
and the mass of the banner-cloth was half-torn by the friction of the sun’s rays as they were struck by the frost-like moonlight.

Then Rāma, his face bright with the joy of being beheld for the first time by his mother, bowed from afar with his face deeply inclined in deep respect for the gods, as she fell from heaven in her chariot like the falling goddess Khaśā, her final garment raised high.

He gave that armor of the Lord of the Three Worlds— which was piled up with heaps of gems, its vastness revealed by being cast down by uplifted hands, from which a fragrance issued forth clinging within it,
and which provided a touch of pleasure to the eyes of the Lord of the Gods as they reached out over all his limbs.

When he descended to the earth, the armor made by Mātali— once worn on the chest of the Lord of the Gods, which had been repeatedly polished by the touch of his hand, and which had become slightly loose on the chest of Rāghava due to the emaciation caused by separation from Sītā—
was fitted to him as a suit of mail for his ascent to the chariot.
Accompanied by the sons of Nīlaravi, the son of Sumitrā spoke to Rāghava: "Having fixed your hand upon the earth, which bears the weight of the bow just now broken,
let your bow rest— its string loosened and slipping from the mouth of the notch."

O Āirā, behold my disgrace! Do not direct your wrath toward the Ten-faced one, who is as heavy as the son of the Sun (Yama) upon the dark [cloud]; rather, abandon your towering indignation at the slaying of the Ten-faced one.
A forest-dwelling elephant may strike down a high bank, but it does not crush the riverbank’s marshy ground, as if it were level earth.
Was it not heard by Rāvaṇa that even with a mere sidelong glance,
the powerful Tisraṇa (the Three-Eyed One) could burn the city of Tripura? Therefore,
having transgressed the forehead of the Ten-Faced One— which was already moistened by sweat rising from the anger of his gaze— what command of the Three-Eyed One could the gods not carry out?
The Lord of the Raghus, whose son [Sugrīva] has been inflamed like the blue sun, replies respectfully to Lakṣmaṇa: "My heart trusts in the resolve you have expressed;
for one who has himself slain the Ten-faced [Rāvaṇa], will my arm not be as capable as a burden?"
By the destruction of the insolent Kumbha and the unbearable Indrajit,

and by slaying the Ten-necked one— who was like a forest elephant fallen before the lion— at the very mouth of the battle, as he was cutting off the speech of the Ten-faced one who had begun to speak; [do not take away my life].
The shower of arrows began to uproot the army of monkeys from its foremost ranks; then,
as both sides were watched by the gods fleeing from the path of the arrows,
the battle between Rāma and the Ten-faced one became equal in intensity, heavy with the prospect of a simultaneous death.
Drawing his bow, whose string was formed by the rays of the jewels in his earrings,
the Ten-faced One first released an arrow at Rāma’s chest; though he was already struck by grief for his fallen kinsman,
the Lord of the Raghus, though steadfast, was thus made to tremble.
Just as he made the entire triple world tremble as if it were not distinct from himself,

so too did the arrow of Raghunātha pass through the mass of palm trees, having traversed the heap of Daśagrīva’s arms— each arm appearing like a pillar, with its bracelets clashing together in rapid succession.
One bowstring is fixed with an arrow drawn back by force until it reaches the very end;
another is drawn level with the middle of the Rakshasa king; and another is light-handed with an arrow released as soon as it is fixed, its string attached firmly to the curved part of the bow.
The bow of Rāma is seen with arrows released by itself and its wide belly drawn into a circle;
even as the left arm remains extended, the right hand has fallen toward the crooked region,
and thus the arrows are seen fixed within the intervals between them.
By the arrow dispatched by the Ten-faced One, Rāghava’s heart— though already scorched by the constant separation from Sītā,
held together by fortitude, and split asunder by grief— was not even perceived;
and by the arrow sent by the Lord of the Raghus, the heart of the Rakshasa lord who had come forward was likewise not perceived.

His forehead is split, yet his clear frown is not yet fully formed; therefore, his mass of faces— rendered helpless by fainting, with eyes filled by streams of blood— has wandered again and again, fluttering over the tips of his arms.
Then he angrily discharged an arrow whose feathers were scorched by the fire of his eye and whose shaft was joined to the curve of a second mouth drawn back in wrath;
that arrow, resembling the fire of destruction, filled the ten directions with its thousands of rays.
Like the solar disc eclipsed at midday by the mouth of Rāhu, the lord of the Raghus,
though possessing great fortitude, beheld the ten-faced Rāvaṇa— who was drawing his arrow close with his right hand— as if he were a bed of blooming lotuses.

Rāma fixes his arrow; the fortune of the Rākṣasas turns away from Vibhīṣaṇa; and at that very moment, Sītā’s left eye throbs, portending the destruction of the Ten-faced one, while the Lord of the Raghus’ right eye twitches.
The pair of eyes of Vibhīṣaṇa, which had been gladdened by the news of his kinsmen’s victory over Rāvaṇa,

now quivers; for as the bow with its arrow fixed is being drawn back by him, who holds his infant son upon his lap, the clusters of tears of the celestial brides are wiped away as if by the flight-path of Rāma’s arrows.
But then, that single face of the ten-faced one— though severed by Rāvaṇa with an arrow that had already split Candahāsa,
and though its neck remained unsevered and heavy— was struck down by a single shaft; yet even thus cut, it remained a source of terror for the Ten-faced One.
Like a mass of flames rising from his own body as he emerged from the earth, a multitude of faces issued forth from the ten mouths of that laughing lord of the Rākṣasas at the front of the battle,
appearing like a fire formidable with its crests of flame.
When the Ten-faced one was slain, when the three worlds sighed with relief on all sides,
and when his speech and his frown were cast aside, Rāma lowered his bow; yet she, knowing the prowess of the Lord of the Night-stalkers, remained distressed by the bonds of her grief.
Thinking "He is my mother," Royal Fortune did not abandon even the slain Rāvaṇa; then, within the heart of Vibhīṣaṇa as well,
a flood of tears born of affection for his kinsman was released by her very eyes even before the descendant of Daśaratha.
When the Ten-faced One was slain, Vibhīṣaṇa— whose fame for the immortality of the gods had been disgraced— began to lament,
his hopes dashed by a sorrow exceeding even death: "The very realm of Yama, which you beheld after conquering Death himself, has become a place of pleasure according to your own desires."

O King, how indeed will you appear now, when that very same [body] which was common to all other men has been abandoned by you at the front of the battle with an equal end, solely because of the previous contemptuous treatment shown to it by Kumbhakarṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas?
O King, if I, who am devoted to Dharma, am not released by my kinsmen who share equally in joy and sorrow as you release me, then who among those devoted to Dharma could be counted as superior?
And the Lord of the Raghus, his arms constricted by a roar of grief intensified at the moment of death, cried out in derision.

O Lord, release me, who am like a mountain whose streams are dried up by the heat of summer and whose suffering has reached its peak due to the loss of my kinsmen; then, having fallen at the feet of the Ten-faced one and Kumbhakarṇa,
I shall later touch the head of Meghanāda, my son, when he has departed to the next world.
Even Rāma, who was compassionate toward the cries of the distressed Viśvaṃbhara as he fell, sprawling upon the earth,
commanded the son of the Wind; and when the Ten-faced one was slain, he honored the Lord of the Rākṣasas, anticipating the recovery of Janaka’s daughter.

Sugrīva, too, having seen the interior of the ocean as if it were a mirror for his own reflection, and having accomplished the task of the gods, was dismissed by the Lord of the Raghus; then, with the banner fluttering like a cloud, he turned his chariot toward heaven in the presence of the monkey host. Mātali [did likewise].
Having taken the son of Janaka— who was as pure as gold thrown into the fire—
the Lord of the Raghus returned to his city to make Bharata’s devotion bear fruit; here concludes this [work], which has produced the joy of Rāma through the recovery of Sītā.

The fifth canto, titled "The Five Encounters," in the great poem *The Slaying of the Ten-Faced One* (*Daśamukhavadha*)— composed by the illustrious Pravarasena and based on the work of Kālidāsa, which is marked by passion and brings solace to all people— entitled *The Slaying of Rāvaṇa*, is hereby completed.
Now follow the additional *skandhaka* verses.
At the hour of twilight, having offered his salutation, he loosened his left hand from the mountain-thatch;
laughing, he released the water and formed a cupped handful with one hand.
Even in the weighty business of battle, all [his enemies], though they licked their lips with longing, simply smiled and faded away.
The opportunity for bees has passed when the flower’s fruit is already set;
yet they come and wheel about, their flight across the sky obstructed by Rāma’s arrows—
towering peaks like mountains of jewels, though small, appearing vast as they turn.
The coral sprouts,
with their shimmering luster, gleam like flowers of linked jewels, their tips entwined by trees on revolving mountain whirlpools;
and the rivers, flowing through the clefts of the great mountains, pass by with smooth fish-backs.

The arrows of Rāma, upon which the hoods of serpents clinging to his face were tossed by his breaking rage, agitate him like clouds at the time of universal destruction, make him tremble like the ocean by the winds of doomsday,
and cause him to waste away like the sun at the end of an aeon— thus he suffers while being worshipped by the gods with their arrows.
The ocean, its waters drawn back by Bāṇa, with its shells slightly opened as they were being moistened, is blossoming;
its sandy banks, filled with gems that are opening like blooming lotuses,
have their heads bowed in añjali-joined palms, their faces pained by the arrows.
At the feet of the son of Daśaratha, he fell like a tree cast down by the force of the wind;

he traverses the circumference of the earth, which is pressed by the feet of monkeys, where the ocean waters surge and reach the horizon, where the rows of trees tremble, and where the mountains shake.
The great mountains, their peaks shattered by jagged, uneven rocks, terrify the pairs of kinnaras; with the cries of mountain torrents released, they are uprooted by the monkeys,
while the masses of clouds fall into the ocean waters, struck down by the falling mountains.

As the face of the bridge was being bound together by the cutting of the bolts in the ocean, it seemed as though it were falling forward; even upon hearing the clamor, the great army of monkeys became instantly paralyzed, agitated by fear, while the heart of Daśānana [Rāvaṇa] grew despondent.

The arrows of Rāma, discharged with impetuosity, produce a thrill throughout the body of the Ten-necked One— just as the rays of the moon, which have a dark face at night, which are a joy to behold as they dispel the garment of darkness, and which possess necklaces of scattered rays, produce a thrill like a breast when it is being massaged during the bloom of youth.
The arrows released from the bow drawn by hands made precious by the touch of Janaka’s daughter’s breasts—
these and more are the *skandhaka* verses.
